name: Cardiac Conduction System
shortExplanation: The heart's built-in electrical wiring that sets the beat — starting at the SA node and traveling through the AV node to the ventricles.

sections.purpose: Generate and coordinate each heartbeat. The SA node (natural pacemaker) fires, the impulse pauses at the AV node to let the ventricles fill, then travels down the bundle of His and Purkinje fibers to contract the ventricles.
sections.careConsiderations: Where the signal fails maps to the arrhythmia: SA node problems cause bradycardia; AV node/His block causes heart block; abnormal ventricular foci cause VT/VF. This system is the target of pacemakers, ablation, and rate/rhythm drugs.

name: Coronary Arteries
shortExplanation: The vessels that supply the heart muscle itself with oxygen-rich blood — the ones that get blocked in a heart attack.

sections.purpose: Deliver oxygenated blood to the myocardium. The left main branches into the LAD (anterior wall) and circumflex (lateral wall); the right coronary artery (RCA) supplies the inferior wall and, in most people, the SA and AV nodes.
sections.careConsiderations: ECG lead groupings map to territories (inferior II/III/aVF ≈ RCA; anterior V1–V4 ≈ LAD; lateral I/aVL/V5–V6 ≈ circumflex), which helps localize an infarct; RCA involvement often causes bradycardia and heart block.

name: Heart Chambers
shortExplanation: The heart's four rooms — two atria that receive blood and two ventricles that pump it — working as a right and left pump in series.

sections.purpose: Move blood through the body. The right atrium and ventricle receive deoxygenated blood and pump it to the lungs; the left atrium and ventricle receive oxygenated blood and pump it to the body — the left ventricle does the hardest work.
sections.careConsiderations: Right-sided failure shows as systemic congestion (JVD, peripheral edema); left-sided failure shows as pulmonary congestion (crackles, dyspnea); the left ventricle's function is summarized by the ejection fraction.

name: Heart Valves
shortExplanation: The four one-way valves that keep blood moving in the right direction through the heart — the mitral, tricuspid, aortic, and pulmonic valves.

sections.purpose: Prevent backflow as the heart pumps. The tricuspid and mitral (AV) valves sit between atria and ventricles; the pulmonic and aortic (semilunar) valves guard the outflow to the lungs and body.
sections.careConsiderations: Valves can narrow (stenosis) or leak (regurgitation), each producing a characteristic murmur; severe disease is treated with repair or replacement (surgical or transcatheter, e.g. TAVR); prosthetic valves often require anticoagulation and raise endocarditis risk.

name: Acute Agitation
shortExplanation: A state of severe restlessness, distress, or aggression that can pose a safety risk to the patient and others and needs prompt, calm management.

sections.presentation: Escalating motor restlessness, loud or threatening speech, pacing, clenched fists, and hostility, which may stem from psychiatric illness, intoxication or withdrawal, delirium, or a medical cause.
sections.typicalTreatments: Begin with verbal de-escalation and a safe, low-stimulation environment. Look for and treat underlying medical causes such as hypoxia, hypoglycemia, or infection. Medications (benzodiazepines and/or antipsychotics) are used when behavioral measures are insufficient, with physical restraint reserved as a last resort with close monitoring.
sections.riskFactors: Psychosis, mania, substance intoxication or withdrawal, delirium and dementia, and untreated pain or metabolic derangements.

name: Acute Coronary Syndrome
shortExplanation: A blocked or critically narrowed coronary artery starving heart muscle of oxygen — the umbrella term for unstable angina, NSTEMI, and STEMI (heart attack).

sections.presentation: Chest pressure or pain (often radiating to the arm/jaw), shortness of breath, diaphoresis, nausea; women, older adults, and diabetics may present atypically.
sections.typicalTreatments: Aspirin plus a second antiplatelet, anticoagulation, nitroglycerin, oxygen if hypoxic, statin; emergent cardiac catheterization (PCI) for STEMI; serial troponins and ECGs.
sections.riskFactors: Smoking, hypertension, diabetes, high cholesterol, family history, older age, obesity.

name: Acute Ischemic Stroke
shortExplanation: A blocked artery cuts off blood flow to part of the brain, causing sudden neurologic deficits. Rapid treatment can save brain tissue.

sections.presentation: Sudden face droop, arm or leg weakness (often one-sided), slurred or garbled speech, vision changes, severe imbalance, or confusion. Time of last known well is critical.
sections.typicalTreatments: Emergent non-contrast CT to rule out bleeding, IV thrombolytics (such as alteplase or tenecteplase) within the treatment window, and mechanical thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion. Careful blood pressure management, glucose control, and swallow screening before oral intake.
sections.riskFactors: Atrial fibrillation, hypertension, diabetes, high cholesterol, smoking, prior stroke or TIA, and older age.

name: Acute Kidney Injury
shortExplanation: A sudden drop in kidney function over hours to days, shown by rising creatinine and/or falling urine output, common in critically ill patients.

sections.presentation: Decreased urine output, rising creatinine and BUN, fluid overload, and electrolyte disturbances such as hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis. Often detected on labs before symptoms.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat the cause, restore perfusion and volume, stop or dose-adjust nephrotoxic drugs, and manage electrolytes and fluid balance. Dialysis or continuous renal replacement therapy for severe or refractory cases.
sections.riskFactors: Hypotension or shock, sepsis, nephrotoxic medications, contrast exposure, major surgery, heart failure, and pre-existing kidney disease.

name: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome
shortExplanation: Sudden, severe lung inflammation that floods the air sacs with fluid, causing dangerously low oxygen levels that often require a ventilator.

sections.presentation: Rapidly worsening shortness of breath and low oxygen levels not explained by heart failure, with diffuse bilateral infiltrates on chest imaging, usually within a week of a known insult such as pneumonia, sepsis, aspiration, or trauma.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat the underlying cause; lung-protective mechanical ventilation using low tidal volumes; prone positioning for severe cases; careful fluid management; and sedation with or without paralysis as needed.
sections.riskFactors: Sepsis, pneumonia, aspiration, severe trauma, pancreatitis, massive transfusion, and inhalation injury.

name: Acute Respiratory Failure
shortExplanation: The lungs suddenly cannot get enough oxygen into the blood (hypoxemic) or clear enough carbon dioxide (hypercapnic), a common reason for ICU admission and intubation.

sections.presentation: Shortness of breath, rapid or labored breathing, use of accessory muscles, restlessness or confusion, and low oxygen saturation. Rising carbon dioxide can cause drowsiness. An arterial blood gas confirms the type and severity.
sections.typicalTreatments: Supplemental oxygen, treating the underlying cause, noninvasive ventilation (BiPAP/CPAP) for selected patients, and intubation with mechanical ventilation when these fail or the airway is at risk.
sections.riskFactors: COPD, pneumonia, heart failure, asthma, ARDS, neuromuscular weakness, opioid overdose, and chest wall or airway problems.

name: Alcohol Withdrawal
shortExplanation: The set of symptoms that appear when a person dependent on alcohol suddenly stops or reduces drinking, which can become life-threatening.

sections.presentation: Tremor, anxiety, agitation, sweating, nausea, tachycardia, and hypertension begin within hours. More severe stages include hallucinations, withdrawal seizures, and delirium tremens, which features confusion, severe autonomic instability, and can be fatal.
sections.typicalTreatments: Benzodiazepines are the mainstay, often dosed using a symptom-triggered approach guided by the CIWA-Ar scale. Add thiamine (before glucose) to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, along with IV fluids, electrolyte correction, and a calm monitored environment.
sections.riskFactors: Long-term heavy alcohol use, prior withdrawal episodes or seizures, prior delirium tremens, and abrupt cessation.

name: Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome
shortExplanation: The set of symptoms that appear when a person who drinks heavily suddenly stops, ranging from tremors and anxiety to seizures and life-threatening delirium tremens.

sections.presentation: Tremors, anxiety, sweating, fast heart rate, hypertension, nausea, and insomnia within hours to days of the last drink. Severe cases progress to hallucinations, seizures, and delirium tremens (confusion, agitation, fever, and autonomic instability).
sections.typicalTreatments: Benzodiazepines titrated to symptoms (often using a scoring tool such as CIWA-Ar), a calm and monitored environment, IV fluids, thiamine before glucose, and correction of electrolytes (magnesium, potassium, phosphorus). ICU care for severe delirium tremens.
sections.riskFactors: Long-standing heavy alcohol use, prior withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens, and abrupt cessation, often during hospitalization for another reason.

name: Aortic Stenosis
shortExplanation: The aortic valve narrows and stiffens, forcing the heart to work harder to push blood out — leading to chest pain, fainting, and heart failure as it worsens.

sections.presentation: Exertional chest pain, syncope, and dyspnea; a harsh systolic ejection murmur radiating to the carotids; narrowed pulse pressure in severe disease.
sections.typicalTreatments: Valve replacement when symptomatic or severe — surgical (SAVR) or transcatheter (TAVR); careful management of blood pressure and volume; avoid abrupt vasodilation.
sections.riskFactors: Older age (calcific degeneration), bicuspid aortic valve, rheumatic heart disease, chronic kidney disease.

name: Apnea of Prematurity
shortExplanation: Pauses in breathing in premature infants caused by an immature respiratory control center in the brain.

sections.presentation: Breathing pauses, often lasting 20 seconds or longer or shorter pauses accompanied by a slow heart rate or drop in oxygen saturation, in a preterm infant.
sections.typicalTreatments: Gentle stimulation, caffeine to stimulate the respiratory center, and respiratory support such as CPAP when needed. Continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring is essential, and new or worsening apnea should prompt evaluation for infection or other causes.
sections.riskFactors: Prematurity (more frequent the earlier the gestational age); apnea may also be worsened by infection, anemia, or reflux.

name: Aspiration Pneumonia
shortExplanation: Lung infection or inflammation that develops after inhaling food, stomach contents, or secretions into the airways, common in patients with impaired swallowing or reduced consciousness.

sections.presentation: Cough, fever, shortness of breath, low oxygen, and purulent sputum, often after a witnessed aspiration event or in a patient at risk. Infiltrates typically appear in dependent lung regions.
sections.typicalTreatments: Supplemental oxygen and airway support, suctioning, and antibiotics guided by severity and risk. Supportive care and treatment of respiratory failure as needed. Swallow evaluation and aspiration precautions to prevent recurrence.
sections.riskFactors: Impaired swallowing, stroke, decreased consciousness, sedation, tube feeding, gastroesophageal reflux, and intubation or extubation.

name: Atrial Fibrillation
shortExplanation: An irregular, often rapid heart rhythm originating in the atria that increases the risk of stroke and can reduce the heart's pumping efficiency.

sections.presentation: Irregularly irregular pulse, palpitations, fatigue, sometimes asymptomatic and found incidentally on telemetry.
sections.typicalTreatments: Rate control (beta-blockers, amiodarone), rhythm control (antiarrhythmics, cardioversion), anticoagulation (warfarin or other agents) to reduce stroke risk.
sections.riskFactors: Advanced age, hypertension, heart failure, hyperthyroidism, excessive alcohol use.

name: Bronchiolitis
shortExplanation: A common lower respiratory infection in infants, most often from RSV, that inflames the small airways and causes wheezing and difficulty breathing.

sections.presentation: Begins with runny nose and cough, then progresses to wheezing, tachypnea, nasal flaring, retractions, and feeding difficulty in a child under 2 years. Apnea can occur in young infants.
sections.typicalTreatments: Mainly supportive: nasal suctioning to clear secretions, adequate hydration, and supplemental oxygen for low saturations. Bronchodilators and steroids are not routinely effective. Monitor respiratory status and hydration closely.
sections.riskFactors: Age under 2 years (especially under 6 months), prematurity, RSV season, secondhand smoke exposure, and daycare attendance.

name: Cardiac Arrest
shortExplanation: The heart abruptly stops pumping effectively, so blood flow to the brain and body ceases — reversible only with immediate CPR and ACLS.

sections.presentation: Sudden unresponsiveness, no pulse, and no normal breathing (or only gasping). Underlying rhythm may be shockable (VF/pulseless VT) or non-shockable (asystole/PEA).
sections.typicalTreatments: Immediate high-quality CPR, defibrillation for shockable rhythms, epinephrine per ACLS, advanced airway, and identifying/treating reversible causes (the Hs and Ts).
sections.riskFactors: Coronary artery disease/MI, heart failure, severe electrolyte disturbance, hypoxia, drug overdose, prior arrest.

name: Cardiac Tamponade
shortExplanation: Fluid building up in the sac around the heart squeezes it so it can't fill properly — a life-threatening emergency that drops blood pressure fast.

sections.presentation: Beck's triad (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins), pulsus paradoxus, tachycardia, dyspnea, low-voltage ECG or electrical alternans.
sections.typicalTreatments: Emergent pericardiocentesis or surgical drainage, IV fluids as a temporizing measure to support filling, treat the underlying cause.
sections.riskFactors: Pericarditis, chest trauma, recent cardiac procedure, malignancy, aortic dissection, post-MI wall rupture.

name: Cardiogenic Shock
shortExplanation: The heart is too weak to pump enough blood to meet the body's needs — organs start to fail from poor perfusion. Most often follows a large heart attack.

sections.presentation: Hypotension, cool/mottled extremities, weak pulses, altered mental status, low urine output, pulmonary congestion, rising lactate.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat the cause (e.g. urgent revascularization for MI), inotropes (dobutamine), vasopressors, and mechanical support such as an intra-aortic balloon pump in severe cases.
sections.riskFactors: Large myocardial infarction, advanced heart failure, severe arrhythmia, acute valve failure.

name: Cellulitis
shortExplanation: A bacterial infection of the skin and underlying tissue that causes a spreading area of redness, warmth, and swelling.

sections.presentation: Warm, red, swollen, tender skin with poorly defined borders, most often on a lower leg; may have fever, chills, and red streaking toward lymph nodes.
sections.typicalTreatments: Antibiotics targeting skin bacteria, limb elevation, marking the border of redness to track spread, and pain control.
sections.riskFactors: Breaks in the skin, edema and venous insufficiency, diabetes, obesity, and lymphedema.

name: Chemotherapy Extravasation
shortExplanation: The accidental leakage of chemotherapy from the vein into surrounding tissue during infusion. With vesicant drugs this can cause severe pain, blistering, and tissue death.

sections.presentation: Burning or pain, swelling, redness, and lack of blood return at the IV site during or after infusion. Vesicant extravasation can progress over days to blistering, ulceration, and necrosis.
sections.typicalTreatments: Stop the infusion immediately while leaving the catheter in place to aspirate residual drug, then remove it and elevate the limb. Apply cold or warm compresses and give a specific antidote depending on the drug, mark and photograph the area, and involve the provider and pharmacy; surgery may be needed for severe injury.
sections.riskFactors: Vesicant drugs such as anthracyclines and vinca alkaloids, small or fragile peripheral veins, poor catheter placement, patient movement, and infusing vesicants peripherally rather than through a central line or port.

name: CHF Exacerbation
shortExplanation: Acute worsening of heart failure symptoms, often from fluid overload.

sections.presentation: Dyspnea, orthopnea, crackles on lung auscultation, jugular venous distension, peripheral edema.
sections.typicalTreatments: Loop diuretics (furosemide), beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, fluid and sodium restriction.
sections.riskFactors: Prior heart failure, uncontrolled hypertension, medication/dietary non-adherence.

name: Chronic Kidney Disease
shortExplanation: A gradual, long-term loss of kidney function; at its end stage (ESRD) it requires dialysis or a transplant.

sections.presentation: Often silent early on; later fatigue, edema, anemia, itching, poor appetite, and mineral and bone disease. It is staged by the GFR.
sections.typicalTreatments: Control blood pressure and diabetes, avoid nephrotoxins, manage anemia with ESAs and iron, use phosphate binders, and adjust diet. End-stage disease requires dialysis or transplant.
sections.riskFactors: Diabetes, hypertension, older age, cardiovascular disease, family history, and repeated episodes of acute kidney injury.

name: Clostridioides difficile Infection
shortExplanation: An antibiotic-associated intestinal infection that causes profuse watery diarrhea and is spread by spores.

sections.presentation: Frequent watery diarrhea, abdominal cramping, fever, and an elevated white blood cell count, typically after recent antibiotic use.
sections.typicalTreatments: Stop the offending antibiotic when possible and treat with oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin (metronidazole in select cases), plus fluids. Use contact precautions with soap-and-water hand hygiene, since alcohol gel does not kill the spores. Fecal transplant is used for recurrences.
sections.riskFactors: Recent antibiotics, hospitalization, older age, and proton pump inhibitor use.

name: COPD Exacerbation
shortExplanation: Acute worsening of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease symptoms — increased shortness of breath, cough, and sputum production, often triggered by infection.

sections.presentation: Increased dyspnea, wheezing, increased sputum production or change in sputum color, use of accessory muscles, low oxygen saturation.
sections.typicalTreatments: Bronchodilators (albuterol), corticosteroids, supplemental oxygen, antibiotics if infection is suspected, possibly BiPAP or intubation in severe cases.
sections.riskFactors: Smoking history, respiratory infection, air pollution exposure, poor medication adherence.

name: Croup
shortExplanation: A viral infection that swells the upper airway in young children, producing a distinctive barking cough and noisy breathing.

sections.presentation: A seal-like barking cough, hoarse voice, and inspiratory stridor, often worse at night and preceded by cold symptoms. Retractions and stridor at rest signal more severe airway narrowing.
sections.typicalTreatments: Corticosteroids such as dexamethasone reduce airway swelling in most cases, and nebulized racemic epinephrine is added for moderate to severe stridor. Keep the child calm, since agitation worsens obstruction, and provide humidified air and oxygen as needed.
sections.riskFactors: Age 6 months to 3 years, fall and winter viral season, and prior episodes of croup.

name: Deep Vein Thrombosis
shortExplanation: A blood clot in a deep vein, usually of the leg, that can break loose and travel to the lungs as a pulmonary embolism.

sections.presentation: Unilateral leg swelling, pain or tenderness, warmth, and redness, most often in the calf; some clots are asymptomatic.
sections.typicalTreatments: Anticoagulation (heparin or LMWH transitioning to oral agents) and leg elevation. Do not massage the affected limb, which could dislodge the clot.
sections.riskFactors: Immobility, recent surgery, cancer, hormone therapy, prior clots, and obesity - reflecting the Virchow triad of stasis, hypercoagulability, and vessel injury.

name: Diabetic Foot Ulcer
shortExplanation: A wound on the foot of a person with diabetes, driven by nerve damage and poor circulation, that heals slowly and can become infected.

sections.presentation: Often painless (because of neuropathy) ulcers over pressure points such as the sole or toes, frequently with surrounding callus; may show infection or poor healing.
sections.typicalTreatments: Offloading pressure from the wound, debridement, moist dressings, glucose control, treating infection, and assessing blood flow. Watch for underlying bone infection (osteomyelitis).
sections.riskFactors: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy, peripheral arterial disease, poor glucose control, foot deformity, and prior ulcers.

name: Diabetic Ketoacidosis
shortExplanation: A serious complication of diabetes where the body produces high levels of blood acids (ketones) due to insufficient insulin — a medical emergency requiring prompt treatment.

sections.presentation: Hyperglycemia, fruity-smelling breath, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing (Kussmaul respirations), altered mental status in severe cases.
sections.typicalTreatments: IV fluids, IV insulin infusion, potassium replacement (insulin drives potassium into cells), correction of the underlying trigger (e.g. infection, missed insulin doses).
sections.riskFactors: Missed insulin doses, infection, new-onset type 1 diabetes, physiologic stress (illness, surgery).

name: Eclampsia
shortExplanation: The onset of seizures in a woman with preeclampsia, representing a life-threatening obstetric emergency for mother and baby.

sections.presentation: Generalized tonic-clonic seizures in a pregnant or recently delivered woman with preeclampsia, often preceded by severe headache, visual disturbances, and hyperreflexia.
sections.typicalTreatments: Protect the airway and prevent injury during the seizure, give magnesium sulfate to control and prevent further seizures, control severe hypertension, and expedite delivery once the mother is stabilized.
sections.riskFactors: Untreated or severe preeclampsia, and the same risk factors as preeclampsia.

name: Febrile Neutropenia
shortExplanation: A fever in a patient with a very low neutrophil count, treated as an oncologic emergency. Because the immune system is impaired, infection can become life-threatening within hours.

sections.presentation: A single oral temperature at or above roughly 38.3 degrees Celsius, or a sustained temperature around 38 degrees, in a neutropenic patient. Localizing signs of infection may be minimal, and the patient can deteriorate quickly to sepsis and shock.
sections.typicalTreatments: Draw blood cultures and a full workup, then start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics that cover Pseudomonas without delay, ideally within about an hour. Support hemodynamics, consider growth factors, and adjust antibiotics based on cultures and the clinical course.
sections.riskFactors: Recent chemotherapy (highest risk at the neutrophil nadir), deeper and longer neutropenia, indwelling catheters, mucositis, and older age or comorbidities.

name: Febrile Seizure
shortExplanation: A convulsion triggered by fever in a young child, usually brief and harmless, occurring most often between 6 months and 5 years of age.

sections.presentation: A generalized seizure during a febrile illness, typically lasting a few minutes, followed by drowsiness. Simple febrile seizures are brief, generalized, and do not recur within 24 hours; complex ones are prolonged, focal, or recurrent.
sections.typicalTreatments: Protect the airway and prevent injury, control the fever, and identify and treat the underlying infection. Simple febrile seizures are self-limited and generally do not require antiseizure medication. Reassure and educate caregivers.
sections.riskFactors: Age 6 months to 5 years, high or rapidly rising fever, viral infections, and a family history of febrile seizures.

name: Gastrointestinal Bleed
shortExplanation: Bleeding anywhere along the digestive tract, which can range from slow and hidden to rapid and life-threatening.

sections.presentation: Upper GI bleeds cause vomiting of blood or coffee-ground material and black tarry stools (melena); lower GI bleeds cause bright red blood per rectum. Large bleeds cause fatigue, low blood pressure, and a fast heart rate.
sections.typicalTreatments: IV access and fluids, blood transfusion as needed, proton pump inhibitors, endoscopy to locate and treat the source, and holding anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs.
sections.riskFactors: NSAID or aspirin use, anticoagulation, peptic ulcer disease, liver disease with varices, and H. pylori infection.

name: HELLP Syndrome
shortExplanation: A severe variant of preeclampsia defined by Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, and Low Platelets that can rapidly threaten the mother's life.

sections.presentation: Right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, nausea and vomiting, malaise, and headache, often with hypertension. Labs show breakdown of red cells, elevated liver enzymes, and a falling platelet count.
sections.typicalTreatments: Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis, blood pressure control, correction of coagulation problems, corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity when preterm, and prompt delivery.
sections.riskFactors: Preeclampsia, prior HELLP, and multiparity; it can occur even when blood pressure elevation is only mild.

name: Hemorrhagic Stroke
shortExplanation: Bleeding into or around the brain from a ruptured vessel, causing sudden neurologic deficits and dangerous pressure on brain tissue.

sections.presentation: Sudden severe headache (often described as the worst ever), vomiting, decreased level of consciousness, focal weakness or speech changes, seizures, and signs of rising intracranial pressure.
sections.typicalTreatments: Emergent CT to confirm and locate bleeding, tight blood pressure control, reversal of anticoagulation, and management of intracranial pressure (hyperosmolar therapy, head-of-bed elevation). Neurosurgical intervention for select cases.
sections.riskFactors: Hypertension, anticoagulant use, aneurysm or arteriovenous malformation, older age, and heavy alcohol use.

name: Hyperkalemia
shortExplanation: A high blood potassium level that can cause dangerous heart rhythm changes and is common in kidney failure.

sections.presentation: Often no symptoms; may cause muscle weakness. Cardiac effects include peaked T waves, a widening QRS, and risk of fatal arrhythmias.
sections.typicalTreatments: IV calcium to stabilize the heart; insulin with glucose and inhaled albuterol to shift potassium into cells; and removal of potassium with diuretics, binders (SPS or patiromer), or dialysis.
sections.riskFactors: Kidney disease, potassium-sparing drugs and ACE inhibitors, tissue breakdown, acidosis, and large blood transfusions.

name: Hypertensive Crisis
shortExplanation: Severely elevated blood pressure. When it starts damaging organs (brain, heart, kidneys) it's an emergency needing carefully controlled lowering.

sections.presentation: Very high BP (often >180/120); emergency if with target-organ signs: headache, vision changes, chest pain, shortness of breath, confusion, or neuro deficits.
sections.typicalTreatments: Hypertensive emergency: IV agents (e.g. nicardipine, labetalol) with gradual, controlled BP reduction to avoid hypoperfusion; hypertensive urgency: oral agents and close follow-up.
sections.riskFactors: Poorly controlled or untreated hypertension, medication non-adherence, kidney disease, stimulant use.

name: Hypoglycemia
shortExplanation: A low blood glucose level that can quickly cause confusion and, if untreated, loss of consciousness or seizures.

sections.presentation: Shakiness, sweating, palpitations, and hunger, progressing to confusion and, in severe cases, loss of consciousness or seizures. It is typically defined as glucose below about 70 mg/dL.
sections.typicalTreatments: Give fast-acting oral carbohydrate (juice or glucose tablets) if the patient is awake and able to swallow; use IV dextrose or IM glucagon if they cannot. Recheck glucose and re-treat as needed (the rule of 15).
sections.riskFactors: Insulin or sulfonylureas, missed meals, kidney disease, alcohol, and tighter glucose targets.

name: Hyponatremia
shortExplanation: A low blood sodium level, the most common electrolyte disorder, which in severe cases causes brain swelling.

sections.presentation: Headache, nausea, confusion, and lethargy; severe or rapid drops can cause seizures and cerebral edema.
sections.typicalTreatments: Depends on the cause and fluid status - fluid restriction, treating the underlying cause, or careful hypertonic saline for severe symptoms. Correct slowly to avoid osmotic demyelination.
sections.riskFactors: SIADH, heart failure, cirrhosis, diuretics, excess water intake, and older age.

name: Hypovolemic Shock
shortExplanation: Shock caused by a large loss of blood or fluid, so there is not enough volume to perfuse the organs.

sections.presentation: Fast, weak pulse, low blood pressure, cool and clammy skin, rapid breathing, thirst, low urine output, and confusion. With hemorrhage there may be obvious or hidden bleeding.
sections.typicalTreatments: Stop the source of loss (control bleeding), rapid IV fluid or blood product resuscitation, and treat the underlying cause. Massive transfusion protocol for severe hemorrhage. Vasopressors are a temporizing measure, not a substitute for volume.
sections.riskFactors: Trauma, gastrointestinal or surgical bleeding, ruptured aneurysm, severe vomiting or diarrhea, burns, and diabetic ketoacidosis.

name: Increased Intracranial Pressure
shortExplanation: Dangerously high pressure inside the skull that reduces blood flow to the brain and can cause brain tissue to shift or herniate.

sections.presentation: Headache, vomiting, decreased level of consciousness, and pupil changes. Late signs include the Cushing triad (rising blood pressure, slow heart rate, irregular breathing) and posturing, which signal impending herniation.
sections.typicalTreatments: Elevate the head of the bed and keep the neck midline, ensure oxygenation and normal carbon dioxide, hyperosmolar therapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline), sedation and analgesia, and CSF drainage via an external ventricular drain. Neurosurgery for select causes.
sections.riskFactors: Traumatic brain injury, hemorrhagic stroke, large ischemic stroke, brain tumor, hydrocephalus, and CNS infection.

name: Infective Endocarditis
shortExplanation: An infection of the heart's inner lining or valves, usually bacterial — dangerous because clumps of infection can break off and travel through the body.

sections.presentation: Fever, new or changed heart murmur, fatigue; classic embolic/immune signs (Janeway lesions, Osler nodes, splinter hemorrhages), positive blood cultures, vegetations on echo.
sections.typicalTreatments: Prolonged IV antibiotics guided by cultures, blood cultures before antibiotics, surgery for valve destruction or persistent infection, monitor for embolic complications.
sections.riskFactors: Prosthetic heart valve, IV drug use, structural heart disease, indwelling lines, prior endocarditis.

name: Kawasaki Disease
shortExplanation: An acute inflammation of blood vessels in young children that, if untreated, can damage the coronary arteries of the heart.

sections.presentation: Fever lasting five or more days plus features such as bilateral conjunctivitis without discharge, cracked red lips and strawberry tongue, rash, swelling and redness of the hands and feet with later peeling, and enlarged cervical lymph nodes. Children are typically very irritable.
sections.typicalTreatments: Intravenous immune globulin (IVIG) and aspirin to reduce inflammation and lower the risk of coronary artery aneurysms. Echocardiography is used to monitor the coronary arteries. Prompt treatment within the first days of illness improves outcomes.
sections.riskFactors: Age under 5 years, male sex, and Asian ancestry, though it occurs in all populations.

name: Malignant Hyperthermia
shortExplanation: A rare, inherited, life-threatening hypermetabolic reaction of skeletal muscle triggered by volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine. It is an anesthesia emergency treated with dantrolene.

sections.presentation: Early signs are an unexplained rise in end-tidal CO2, tachycardia, and masseter or generalized muscle rigidity. Later signs include a rapidly rising temperature, mixed acidosis, hyperkalemia, dark cola-colored urine from rhabdomyolysis, and unstable vital signs.
sections.typicalTreatments: Immediately stop the triggering agent and call for the MH cart, give IV dantrolene, hyperventilate with 100% oxygen, and start active cooling. Treat hyperkalemia and acidosis, support urine output, and monitor for recurrence in the ICU.
sections.riskFactors: Inherited RYR1 or related gene mutation (autosomal dominant), personal or family history of an MH event or of certain muscle disorders, and exposure to volatile anesthetics (such as sevoflurane) or succinylcholine.

name: Mucositis
shortExplanation: Painful inflammation and ulceration of the mucous membranes lining the mouth and GI tract, caused by chemotherapy or radiation. Oral mucositis can make eating, drinking, and swallowing very difficult.

sections.presentation: Redness, soreness, swelling, and ulcers of the mouth and throat, pain with eating or swallowing, and sometimes bleeding. It can extend along the GI tract, causing diarrhea, and open sores create a route for infection.
sections.typicalTreatments: Frequent gentle oral care with a soft brush and bland rinses, topical and systemic analgesia (including opioids for severe pain), treating superimposed infections such as candidiasis, and supporting nutrition and hydration. Cryotherapy (ice chips) during certain infusions can help prevent it.
sections.riskFactors: Chemotherapy (especially agents like fluorouracil and methotrexate), head and neck radiation, high-dose therapy and transplant conditioning, neutropenia, and poor baseline oral hygiene.

name: Necrotizing Enterocolitis
shortExplanation: A serious intestinal disease of mostly premature infants in which the bowel becomes inflamed and can die, sometimes leading to perforation.

sections.presentation: Feeding intolerance, abdominal distension and tenderness, bloody stools, bilious gastric residuals, and systemic signs such as lethargy, apnea, and temperature instability. Abdominal x-ray may show gas within the bowel wall (pneumatosis intestinalis).
sections.typicalTreatments: Stop feeds and rest the gut (NPO), decompress the stomach with a tube, give IV fluids, nutrition, and broad-spectrum antibiotics, and monitor closely. Surgery is needed if the bowel perforates or the infant deteriorates.
sections.riskFactors: Prematurity and low birth weight, formula feeding, rapid advancement of feeds, and conditions reducing intestinal blood flow.

name: Neonatal Hyperbilirubinemia
shortExplanation: A high level of bilirubin in a newborn that causes jaundice, and if severe and untreated can injure the brain.

sections.presentation: Yellowing of the skin and whites of the eyes, typically starting on the face and progressing downward, along with sleepiness or poor feeding when severe. Bilirubin levels are trended against age in hours.
sections.typicalTreatments: Phototherapy to break down bilirubin, ensuring adequate feeding and hydration to promote excretion, and exchange transfusion for dangerously high levels. Very high untreated bilirubin can cause kernicterus, a permanent brain injury.
sections.riskFactors: Prematurity, blood type incompatibility between mother and baby, bruising or cephalohematoma, poor feeding, and a sibling who required phototherapy.

name: Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome
shortExplanation: A breathing disorder of premature newborns caused by a lack of surfactant, which keeps the tiny air sacs in the lungs from staying open.

sections.presentation: Within hours of birth a preterm infant develops tachypnea, grunting, nasal flaring, chest retractions, and cyanosis, with worsening oxygenation.
sections.typicalTreatments: Exogenous surfactant given through the breathing tube, respiratory support with CPAP or mechanical ventilation, and supplemental oxygen. Antenatal corticosteroids given to the mother before preterm birth help prevent it.
sections.riskFactors: Prematurity (the more premature, the higher the risk), maternal diabetes, cesarean delivery without labor, and lack of antenatal steroids.

name: Neonatal Sepsis
shortExplanation: A bloodstream infection in a newborn that can progress rapidly and requires prompt recognition and antibiotics.

sections.presentation: Often subtle and nonspecific: temperature instability (fever or low temperature), poor feeding, lethargy or irritability, apnea, respiratory distress, and poor perfusion. Early-onset appears within the first days of life and late-onset after.
sections.typicalTreatments: Obtain blood cultures and other cultures, then start empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics (commonly ampicillin plus gentamicin) without delay, and provide supportive care for breathing and circulation. Narrow therapy once culture results return.
sections.riskFactors: Maternal group B strep colonization, prolonged rupture of membranes, chorioamnionitis, prematurity, and invasive lines or devices.

name: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome
shortExplanation: A rare but life-threatening reaction to antipsychotic (dopamine-blocking) medications marked by high fever and severe muscle rigidity.

sections.presentation: High fever, generalized lead-pipe muscle rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability (fluctuating blood pressure, tachycardia, sweating). Laboratory tests often show a markedly elevated creatine kinase. It usually develops over days.
sections.typicalTreatments: Immediately stop the offending antipsychotic, provide aggressive supportive care with cooling and IV fluids, and use medications such as dantrolene or bromocriptine in severe cases. Monitor for complications like kidney injury from muscle breakdown.
sections.riskFactors: Starting or increasing antipsychotics, high-potency agents, rapid dose escalation, dehydration, and abruptly stopping dopaminergic medications.

name: Neutropenia
shortExplanation: An abnormally low number of neutrophils, the white blood cells that fight bacterial infection. It is a common effect of chemotherapy and greatly raises infection risk.

sections.presentation: Often asymptomatic until infection develops. Because there are few neutrophils, the usual signs of infection may be blunted, so fever may be the only clue. Severity is graded by the absolute neutrophil count (ANC), with an ANC below 500 considered severe.
sections.typicalTreatments: Treat and prevent infection with meticulous hand hygiene and neutropenic precautions, prompt evaluation of any fever, growth factor support such as filgrastim when indicated, and delaying or dose-reducing chemotherapy when counts are too low.
sections.riskFactors: Cytotoxic chemotherapy (the most common cause), radiation, bone marrow cancers and transplant, certain drugs, and severe infection. Risk of serious infection rises as the count falls and the neutropenic period lengthens.

name: Opioid Withdrawal
shortExplanation: The uncomfortable but usually not life-threatening symptoms that occur when someone dependent on opioids stops or cuts back.

sections.presentation: Anxiety and drug craving, muscle aches, abdominal cramping, nausea, vomiting and diarrhea, runny nose and tearing, yawning, sweating, dilated pupils, goosebumps, and restlessness. Symptoms are very distressing but rarely dangerous in otherwise healthy adults.
sections.typicalTreatments: Medications such as buprenorphine or methadone ease withdrawal and support recovery, and clonidine helps with autonomic symptoms. Symptomatic care addresses nausea, diarrhea, and muscle aches. Severity is often tracked with the COWS scale.
sections.riskFactors: Physical dependence from chronic opioid use, abrupt cessation, and administration of an opioid antagonist such as naloxone or naltrexone.

name: Otitis Media
shortExplanation: A middle ear infection that is one of the most common illnesses of early childhood, causing ear pain and fever.

sections.presentation: Ear pain, tugging at the ear in nonverbal children, fever, irritability, trouble sleeping, and sometimes drainage if the eardrum ruptures. The eardrum appears red, bulging, and poorly mobile on exam.
sections.typicalTreatments: Pain and fever control with acetaminophen or ibuprofen, and antibiotics such as amoxicillin when treatment is indicated. Some cases are observed without antibiotics. Recurrent infections may lead to ear tube placement.
sections.riskFactors: Young age, daycare attendance, bottle feeding while lying down, pacifier use, secondhand smoke, and recent upper respiratory infection.

name: Pediatric Asthma Exacerbation
shortExplanation: An acute flare of asthma in a child, with narrowing of the airways causing wheezing, cough, and increased work of breathing.

sections.presentation: Wheezing, cough, chest tightness, prolonged expiration, retractions, nasal flaring, and use of accessory muscles. Severe attacks may show a silent chest, inability to speak in full sentences, and falling oxygen saturation.
sections.typicalTreatments: Inhaled short-acting bronchodilators (albuterol), often with ipratropium in the acute setting, systemic corticosteroids, and supplemental oxygen. Severe cases may need continuous nebulization or magnesium. Reassess respiratory effort and oxygenation frequently.
sections.riskFactors: Known asthma, viral respiratory infections, allergen or smoke exposure, exercise, cold air, and poor adherence to controller medications.

name: Pediatric Dehydration
shortExplanation: A loss of body fluids in children, often from vomiting and diarrhea, that can progress quickly and become dangerous in infants.

sections.presentation: Dry mucous membranes, decreased urine output and fewer wet diapers, absent tears, sunken eyes, delayed capillary refill, and lethargy. In infants a sunken fontanelle is a sign, and severe cases show tachycardia and low blood pressure.
sections.typicalTreatments: Oral rehydration therapy is preferred for mild to moderate dehydration, given in small frequent amounts. IV fluids are used for severe dehydration, persistent vomiting, or shock. Treat the underlying cause and monitor weight, urine output, and electrolytes.
sections.riskFactors: Gastroenteritis with vomiting and diarrhea, young age, fever, poor oral intake, and limited access to fluids.

name: Pericarditis
shortExplanation: Inflammation of the sac around the heart, causing sharp chest pain that often eases when sitting forward. Usually treatable, but can lead to fluid buildup.

sections.presentation: Sharp, pleuritic chest pain relieved by leaning forward, a pericardial friction rub, and diffuse ST elevation with PR depression on ECG.
sections.typicalTreatments: NSAIDs and colchicine, treat the underlying cause, monitor for progression to a pericardial effusion or tamponade.
sections.riskFactors: Recent viral infection, recent MI (Dressler syndrome), cardiac surgery, autoimmune disease, uremia.

name: Perioperative Hypothermia
shortExplanation: An unintended drop in core body temperature below about 36 degrees Celsius around the time of surgery. Anesthesia impairs the body's ability to hold heat in a cold operating room.

sections.presentation: Low core temperature, shivering on emergence, cold extremities, and patient-reported chilling. It contributes to discomfort and delayed recovery.
sections.typicalTreatments: Active warming with forced-air warming blankets, warmed IV fluids and irrigation, raising the ambient temperature, and covering exposed skin. Prewarming before induction helps prevent it.
sections.riskFactors: General or neuraxial anesthesia, cold operating rooms, long procedures, large exposed surgical fields, extremes of age, low body weight, and infusion of cool fluids. Consequences include increased surgical site infection, coagulopathy and bleeding, cardiac events, and prolonged drug effects.

name: Placental Abruption
shortExplanation: Premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall before delivery, which can cut off the baby's oxygen supply and cause dangerous maternal bleeding.

sections.presentation: Sudden painful vaginal bleeding, a firm, tender, or rigid uterus, frequent contractions, and often a nonreassuring or absent fetal heart rate. Bleeding may be concealed behind the placenta, so blood loss can be underestimated.
sections.typicalTreatments: Continuous fetal and maternal monitoring, IV access and fluid or blood resuscitation, and prompt delivery (often cesarean) when the mother or fetus is unstable. Watch for disseminated intravascular coagulation.
sections.riskFactors: Maternal hypertension or preeclampsia, abdominal trauma, cocaine or tobacco use, prior abruption, advanced maternal age, and multiple gestation.

name: Pneumonia
shortExplanation: An infection of the lung tissue that fills air sacs with fluid or pus, causing cough, fever, and difficulty breathing.

sections.presentation: Cough (often productive), fever, shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain, crackles on auscultation, and low oxygen saturation. Older adults may present with new confusion or falls rather than classic symptoms.
sections.typicalTreatments: Antibiotics guided by whether it is community- or hospital-acquired, supplemental oxygen, fluids, antipyretics, and pulmonary hygiene such as incentive spirometry and early mobility.
sections.riskFactors: Older age, smoking, COPD, immobility, aspiration risk, recent hospitalization, and immunosuppression.

name: Postoperative Nausea and Vomiting
shortExplanation: Nausea and vomiting occurring in the first day or so after anesthesia and surgery. It is one of the most common and distressing complications for surgical patients.

sections.presentation: Nausea, retching, and vomiting in the recovery unit or on the ward after surgery, which can delay discharge and, rarely, cause aspiration or wound strain.
sections.typicalTreatments: Multimodal prophylaxis and treatment with antiemetics from different classes (for example a serotonin antagonist plus dexamethasone), reducing opioids with multimodal analgesia, adequate hydration, and using regional or total IV anesthesia in high-risk patients.
sections.riskFactors: Female sex, nonsmoking status, history of PONV or motion sickness, and postoperative opioid use are the main risk factors (Apfel score); volatile anesthetics, nitrous oxide, and certain surgery types also increase risk.

name: Postpartum Hemorrhage
shortExplanation: Excessive bleeding after childbirth, a leading cause of maternal death that requires rapid recognition and treatment.

sections.presentation: Heavy vaginal bleeding after delivery, a soft (boggy) or poorly contracted uterus, passage of large clots, and signs of blood loss such as tachycardia, hypotension, and pallor.
sections.typicalTreatments: The cause is often summarized as the four Ts: Tone (uterine atony, the most common), Trauma (lacerations), Tissue (retained placenta), and Thrombin (coagulopathy). Management includes firm fundal massage, uterotonic medications (oxytocin, methylergonovine, misoprostol, carboprost), IV fluids and blood products, and procedures such as uterine tamponade or surgery if bleeding continues.
sections.riskFactors: Uterine atony, prolonged or induced labor, overdistended uterus (large baby, twins, polyhydramnios), retained placenta, operative delivery, and clotting disorders.

name: Preeclampsia
shortExplanation: A pregnancy complication of new high blood pressure with signs of organ stress (such as protein in the urine) after 20 weeks of gestation.

sections.presentation: New-onset hypertension after 20 weeks plus proteinuria or other end-organ signs. Warning features include severe headache, visual changes (blurring, flashing lights), right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, hyperreflexia, rapid swelling, and shortness of breath.
sections.typicalTreatments: Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis in severe disease, antihypertensives such as labetalol, hydralazine, or nifedipine for dangerous blood pressures, corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity if preterm, and ultimately delivery, which is the definitive treatment.
sections.riskFactors: First pregnancy, prior preeclampsia, chronic hypertension, diabetes, kidney disease, obesity, multiple gestation, and extremes of maternal age.

name: Pressure Injury
shortExplanation: Localized damage to skin and underlying tissue from sustained pressure over a bony prominence, staged by depth.

sections.presentation: Staged as: Stage 1 (intact skin with non-blanchable redness), Stage 2 (partial-thickness loss or blister), Stage 3 (full-thickness loss into fat), and Stage 4 (exposed muscle, tendon, or bone). Unstageable wounds are covered by slough or eschar; deep tissue injury shows persistent maroon or purple discoloration.
sections.typicalTreatments: Pressure redistribution with repositioning and support surfaces, offloading, moisture and nutrition management, stage-appropriate dressings, and debridement of nonviable tissue.
sections.riskFactors: Immobility, poor nutrition, moisture and incontinence, friction and shear, reduced sensation, and poor perfusion; risk is screened with tools such as the Braden scale.

name: Pulmonary Embolism
shortExplanation: A blockage in a lung artery, usually caused by a blood clot that traveled from the legs (DVT) — a potentially life-threatening emergency.

sections.presentation: Sudden shortness of breath, chest pain (often pleuritic), tachycardia, low oxygen saturation, sometimes hemoptysis.
sections.typicalTreatments: Anticoagulation (heparin, then often transitioned to an oral anticoagulant), thrombolytics in severe/massive PE, supportive oxygen therapy.
sections.riskFactors: Immobility, recent surgery, DVT history, cancer, pregnancy, clotting disorders.

name: Retinopathy of Prematurity
shortExplanation: Abnormal growth of blood vessels in the eyes of premature infants that, if severe, can lead to retinal detachment and blindness.

sections.presentation: There are no outward symptoms; the condition is found on screening dilated eye exams performed on at-risk preterm infants. Disease is graded by stage and location within the retina.
sections.typicalTreatments: Many mild cases resolve on their own with monitoring. Advanced disease is treated with laser therapy or anti-VEGF injections to prevent retinal detachment. Careful oxygen management helps reduce the risk.
sections.riskFactors: Prematurity and low birth weight, prolonged or high supplemental oxygen exposure, and unstable oxygen saturations.

name: Sepsis
shortExplanation: A life-threatening response to infection that can lead to organ dysfunction and shock if not treated quickly.

sections.presentation: Fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnea, altered mental status, hypotension in severe cases (septic shock).
sections.typicalTreatments: Broad-spectrum antibiotics, IV fluid resuscitation, vasopressors if hypotension persists, source control of the underlying infection.
sections.riskFactors: Immunosuppression, indwelling catheters/lines, recent surgery, advanced age, chronic illness.

name: Septic Shock
shortExplanation: The most severe form of sepsis, where infection causes dangerously low blood pressure and poor organ perfusion that persist despite fluids and require vasopressors.

sections.presentation: Signs of infection plus persistent low blood pressure needing vasopressors to maintain perfusion, an elevated lactate, fever or low temperature, fast heart rate, altered mental status, mottled skin, and low urine output.
sections.typicalTreatments: Early broad-spectrum antibiotics after cultures, IV fluid resuscitation, and vasopressors (norepinephrine first) to maintain a mean arterial pressure goal; source control; and serial lactate measurement following the sepsis bundle.
sections.riskFactors: Older age, immunosuppression, chronic illness, recent surgery or invasive devices, and untreated or severe infection.

name: Serotonin Syndrome
shortExplanation: A potentially life-threatening reaction from too much serotonin activity, usually from combining serotonergic medications.

sections.presentation: A triad of mental status changes (agitation, confusion), autonomic instability (fever, tachycardia, high blood pressure, sweating, dilated pupils), and neuromuscular abnormalities (tremor, hyperreflexia, and clonus that is often more pronounced in the legs). Onset is usually rapid, within hours of a change in serotonergic drugs.
sections.typicalTreatments: Stop all serotonergic agents, provide supportive care with cooling and IV fluids, control agitation and muscle rigidity with benzodiazepines, and use cyproheptadine as a serotonin blocker in more severe cases.
sections.riskFactors: Combining serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, MAO inhibitors, certain opioids like tramadol, triptans, linezolid), overdose, or adding a new serotonergic agent.

name: Small Bowel Obstruction
shortExplanation: A blockage of the small intestine that stops the normal passage of contents, causing pain, vomiting, and distension.

sections.presentation: Crampy abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, and inability to pass stool or gas; bowel sounds may be high-pitched then absent.
sections.typicalTreatments: Bowel rest (nothing by mouth), a nasogastric tube for decompression, IV fluids, and electrolyte correction. Surgery is needed for strangulation or if it does not resolve.
sections.riskFactors: Prior abdominal surgery (adhesions), hernias, tumors, and Crohn disease.

name: Status Epilepticus
shortExplanation: A seizure that lasts too long or repeated seizures without full recovery in between - a neurologic emergency that needs immediate treatment.

sections.presentation: A convulsive seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, or repeated seizures without returning to baseline. Nonconvulsive status may show only altered consciousness and requires EEG to detect.
sections.typicalTreatments: Airway and oxygen support, benzodiazepines as first-line, followed by an antiseizure medication (such as levetiracetam, fosphenytoin, or valproate). Refractory cases may need continuous infusions and intubation. Check and treat glucose and other reversible causes.
sections.riskFactors: Known epilepsy with missed medication, acute brain injury or stroke, infection, metabolic disturbances, alcohol or drug withdrawal, and low glucose.

name: Surgical Site Infection
shortExplanation: An infection at or near a surgical incision occurring after an operation. It is a common and largely preventable surgical complication.

sections.presentation: Redness, warmth, swelling, increasing pain, and purulent drainage at the incision, sometimes with wound dehiscence and fever. It may be superficial or extend to deep tissue or the organ space.
sections.typicalTreatments: Wound cultures, opening and draining the wound when needed, dressing changes, and antibiotics targeted to the organism. Deep or organ-space infections may need return to the operating room.
sections.riskFactors: Diabetes and hyperglycemia, obesity, smoking, prolonged or contaminated surgery, immunosuppression, and lapses in prevention such as mistimed prophylactic antibiotics, hypothermia, or shaving (rather than clipping) the surgical site.

name: Symptomatic Bradycardia
shortExplanation: A heart rate too slow to meet the body's needs — often from a conduction problem (heart block) — causing dizziness, fatigue, or low blood pressure.

sections.presentation: Heart rate typically <60 with symptoms: lightheadedness, fatigue, syncope, hypotension, chest pain, or shortness of breath. ECG may show sinus bradycardia or AV block.
sections.typicalTreatments: Atropine first-line, transcutaneous pacing if atropine fails, dopamine or epinephrine infusion; permanent pacemaker for persistent high-grade block.
sections.riskFactors: Inferior MI, degenerative conduction disease, medications (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, digoxin), hyperkalemia, increased vagal tone.

name: Tumor Lysis Syndrome
shortExplanation: A metabolic emergency in which rapidly dying cancer cells dump their contents into the blood, usually just after starting treatment. The released chemicals can cause dangerous electrolyte swings, kidney failure, and arrhythmias.

sections.presentation: High potassium, high phosphate, high uric acid, and low calcium, leading to nausea, weakness, muscle cramps, tetany, cardiac arrhythmias, seizures, and acute kidney injury with reduced urine output.
sections.typicalTreatments: Aggressive IV hydration, close monitoring of electrolytes and kidney function, uric-acid-lowering therapy with allopurinol or rasburicase, and treatment of hyperkalemia. Cardiac monitoring and, in severe cases, dialysis.
sections.riskFactors: Bulky, rapidly proliferating, treatment-sensitive cancers such as acute leukemias and high-grade lymphomas, high tumor burden, pre-existing kidney impairment, and the initiation of chemotherapy.

name: Upper GI Bleed
shortExplanation: Bleeding from the upper digestive tract (esophagus, stomach, or duodenum) that can range from minor to life-threatening hemorrhage.

sections.presentation: Vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, black tarry stools (melena), and with brisk bleeding, red blood per rectum. Large losses cause lightheadedness, fast heart rate, low blood pressure, and pallor.
sections.typicalTreatments: Large-bore IV access and fluid or blood resuscitation, proton pump inhibitor therapy, and urgent endoscopy to find and control the source. Octreotide and antibiotics for suspected variceal bleeding; transfusion guided by a restrictive strategy for most patients.
sections.riskFactors: Peptic ulcer disease, NSAID or anticoagulant use, H. pylori infection, liver disease with varices, and heavy alcohol use.

name: Urinary Tract Infection
shortExplanation: An infection of the bladder or kidneys; it is a very common reason for admission and can progress to life-threatening urosepsis.

sections.presentation: Burning with urination, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, and cloudy or foul-smelling urine. Flank pain and fever suggest a kidney infection (pyelonephritis); older adults may show new confusion.
sections.typicalTreatments: Antibiotics guided by urine culture, hydration, and removing or changing indwelling catheters when possible.
sections.riskFactors: Female anatomy, indwelling urinary catheters, urinary retention, diabetes, older age, and immobility.

name: Venous Stasis Ulcer
shortExplanation: A chronic lower-leg wound caused by poor vein circulation, and the most common type of leg ulcer.

sections.presentation: Shallow, irregular wounds around the ankle or inner lower leg, with surrounding brown-stained (hemosiderin) and swollen skin; usually mild pain but moderate to heavy drainage.
sections.typicalTreatments: Compression therapy is the cornerstone once adequate arterial flow is confirmed, along with leg elevation, moist wound dressings, and skin care.
sections.riskFactors: Chronic venous insufficiency, prior DVT, obesity, prolonged standing, and older age.

name: Ventricular Fibrillation
shortExplanation: The ventricles quiver chaotically instead of pumping, so there's no effective heartbeat — a form of cardiac arrest that requires immediate CPR and defibrillation.

sections.presentation: Sudden loss of pulse and consciousness; ECG shows disorganized, irregular waveforms with no identifiable QRS complexes.
sections.typicalTreatments: Immediate high-quality CPR and defibrillation (a shockable rhythm), epinephrine and amiodarone per ACLS, and treatment of reversible causes.
sections.riskFactors: Acute MI/ischemia, cardiomyopathy, severe electrolyte imbalance, prolonged QT, prior cardiac arrest.

name: Ventricular Tachycardia
shortExplanation: A fast rhythm arising from the ventricles — it can be stable, or become pulseless and life-threatening. Treatment depends on whether the patient has a pulse and is stable.

sections.presentation: Palpitations, chest pain, shortness of breath, lightheadedness; may deteriorate to loss of pulse. ECG shows a wide-complex, regular, fast rhythm.
sections.typicalTreatments: Pulseless VT: CPR and defibrillation per ACLS. Unstable with a pulse: synchronized cardioversion. Stable: antiarrhythmics such as amiodarone.
sections.riskFactors: Prior MI/scar, cardiomyopathy, electrolyte abnormalities, prolonged QT, structural heart disease.

name: 12-Lead ECG
shortExplanation: A recording of the heart's electrical activity from 12 angles — the key bedside test for diagnosing a heart attack and identifying arrhythmias.

sections.purpose: Capture a detailed electrical snapshot of the heart to detect ischemia/infarction, arrhythmias, conduction blocks, and electrolyte effects.
sections.careConsiderations: Place limb and precordial leads in correct anatomic positions (misplacement mimics pathology); prep skin for a clean signal; minimize motion artifact; get it within 10 minutes for chest pain and compare with prior tracings.

name: Capnography Monitor
shortExplanation: A monitor that measures exhaled carbon dioxide (end-tidal CO2) breath by breath, used to confirm airway placement and watch breathing in real time.

sections.purpose: Continuously measure end-tidal CO2 to confirm and monitor endotracheal tube placement, detect early respiratory depression during sedation, and assess ventilation and the effectiveness of CPR.
sections.careConsiderations: Recognize the normal waveform and values (end-tidal CO2 roughly 35-45 mmHg). A sudden loss of waveform can mean a dislodged tube, disconnection, or cardiac arrest. During procedural sedation it detects hypoventilation earlier than pulse oximetry. Keep the sensor free of secretions and moisture.

name: Cardiac Telemetry Monitor
shortExplanation: Continuous wireless heart-rhythm monitoring that lets staff watch for arrhythmias in real time from a central station.

sections.purpose: Continuously track heart rhythm and rate to catch arrhythmias, ischemic changes, or dangerous rate changes early.
sections.careConsiderations: Place and change electrodes on clean, dry skin; know each patient's alarm parameters and respond to alarms (avoid alarm fatigue); ensure leads stay connected and the battery is charged; correlate any rhythm change with the patient's symptoms and a 12-lead ECG.

name: Defibrillator
shortExplanation: The device that delivers a shock to the heart — used unsynchronized to defibrillate arrest rhythms, or synchronized to cardiovert unstable ones; many also pace.

sections.purpose: Deliver a controlled electrical shock to terminate life-threatening arrhythmias (defibrillation for VF/pulseless VT; synchronized cardioversion for unstable tachyarrhythmias) and provide transcutaneous pacing.
sections.careConsiderations: Ensure pads have good skin contact and clear everyone before discharge ("I'm clear, you're clear"); select sync mode for cardioversion but not for defibrillation; keep it charged and checked each shift; remove medication patches and avoid pad placement over an implanted device.

name: Home Oxygen Therapy
shortExplanation: Supplemental oxygen delivered in the home for patients with chronic low blood oxygen, such as those with advanced COPD or heart failure. It is usually supplied by a concentrator or portable tanks.

sections.purpose: Maintains adequate blood oxygen levels to reduce breathlessness, support organ function, and improve activity tolerance and survival in patients with chronic hypoxemia.
sections.careConsiderations: Deliver oxygen at the prescribed flow through nasal cannula or mask; do not change the rate without an order, since some patients rely on a lower drive to breathe. Teach fire safety strictly (no smoking, flames, or heat sources near oxygen, since it strongly supports combustion), secure tubing to prevent falls, provide skin and nasal care to prevent breakdown, humidify at higher flows, and have a backup plan and supplier contact for equipment or power failure.

name: Implanted Port
shortExplanation: A small device placed under the skin, usually on the chest, connected to a catheter in a large central vein. It gives durable access for chemotherapy, blood draws, and infusions, and is accessed with a special non-coring needle.

sections.purpose: Provides reliable, long-term central venous access for repeated chemotherapy, infusions, transfusions, and blood sampling, sparing peripheral veins and reducing the risk of vesicant extravasation when used correctly.
sections.careConsiderations: Access with a non-coring (Huber) needle using sterile technique, confirm blood return before infusing, and flush per protocol (often with saline and sometimes heparin) to keep it patent. Monitor for infection at the site or bloodstream, occlusion, catheter migration, and (rarely) the needle dislodging from the port during infusion of a vesicant. Teach the patient the signs of infection and how the port is used.

name: Incentive Spirometer
shortExplanation: A handheld breathing device that encourages slow, deep breaths to keep the lungs expanded after surgery or during immobility.

sections.purpose: Promotes deep breathing to prevent atelectasis (collapsed air sacs) and reduce the risk of pneumonia after surgery or with limited mobility.
sections.careConsiderations: Teach the patient to inhale slowly and deeply, hold a few seconds, and aim for a target volume, roughly 10 times per hour while awake. Provide it after pain is controlled and have the patient splint incisions with a pillow when coughing.

name: Intra-Aortic Balloon Pump
shortExplanation: A balloon in the aorta that inflates and deflates with the heartbeat to boost coronary blood flow and ease the heart's workload — used in severe heart failure or cardiogenic shock.

sections.purpose: Provide temporary mechanical circulatory support — inflating in diastole to improve coronary perfusion and deflating in systole to reduce afterload, increasing cardiac output.
sections.careConsiderations: Verify timing to the cardiac cycle (inflation on the dicrotic notch), keep the affected leg straight and monitor distal pulses/perfusion, watch the insertion site for bleeding, monitor platelets and for limb/renal ischemia, and never let the balloon sit idle (clot risk).

name: Mechanical Ventilator
shortExplanation: A machine that delivers breaths through a breathing tube to support or fully take over a patient's breathing when they cannot breathe adequately on their own.

sections.purpose: Support or replace spontaneous breathing by delivering controlled oxygen and pressure, ensuring adequate oxygenation and carbon dioxide removal in respiratory failure, during sedation and paralysis, or after major surgery.
sections.careConsiderations: Confirm tube placement and secure it, monitor settings (mode, tidal volume, rate, FiO2, PEEP) and alarms, and respond promptly to high-pressure or low-pressure alarms. Provide oral care and elevate the head of the bed to reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia, manage sedation to a goal, and assess readiness for weaning with spontaneous breathing trials.

name: Negative Pressure Wound Therapy
shortExplanation: A wound vacuum system that applies gentle suction through a sealed dressing to speed healing of complex wounds.

sections.purpose: A sealed foam or gauze dressing connected to suction removes wound fluid, reduces swelling, and stimulates granulation tissue, helping deep or chronic wounds heal.
sections.careConsiderations: Maintain an airtight seal and the prescribed suction level; monitor canister output and change the dressing per protocol. Watch for bleeding (it should not be placed over exposed vessels or organs) and protect the skin around the seal.

name: Albumin
shortExplanation: The main protein in blood; low levels can flag malnutrition or illness and are linked to poor wound healing.

sections.normalRange: About 3.5-5.0 g/dL.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Low albumin can reflect malnutrition, inflammation, liver disease, or protein loss through the kidneys or gut, and is associated with poor wound healing and edema. It is a marker of nutrition and overall illness rather than a specific diagnosis.

name: Ammonia
shortExplanation: A blood test of a nitrogen waste product that can build up when the liver fails to clear it, contributing to confusion in hepatic encephalopathy.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 15-45 mcg/dL in adults, though reference ranges vary by laboratory and method.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated levels are associated with hepatic encephalopathy and other causes of impaired ammonia clearance. The level does not always correlate tightly with the degree of confusion, so treatment is guided mainly by the clinical picture. Proper sample handling (kept on ice and processed promptly) is important because delays falsely raise results.

name: Arterial Blood Gas
shortExplanation: A blood test drawn from an artery that measures oxygen, carbon dioxide, and acid-base balance to assess how well the lungs and metabolism are working.

sections.abnormalMeaning: Low pH is acidosis, high pH is alkalosis. A high PaCO2 points to respiratory acidosis (inadequate ventilation); a low PaCO2 to respiratory alkalosis. Abnormal HCO3 reflects metabolic disturbances. Low PaO2 or SaO2 indicates hypoxemia. Results guide ventilator settings and treatment of acid-base disorders.

name: Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN)
shortExplanation: A blood test reflecting kidney function and hydration; it measures a nitrogen waste product from protein breakdown.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 7-20 mg/dL.
sections.abnormalMeaning: High with kidney impairment, dehydration, GI bleeding, high protein intake, or tissue breakdown; low with overhydration or liver disease. It is interpreted alongside creatinine, and the BUN-to-creatinine ratio helps identify dehydration-related (prerenal) causes.

name: BNP
shortExplanation: A hormone released when the heart's chambers are stretched by fluid overload — helps confirm and gauge the severity of heart failure.

sections.normalRange: Typically <100 pg/mL for BNP; NT-proBNP cutoffs are higher and rise with age. Interpreted alongside the clinical picture.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated levels suggest cardiac wall stretch from heart failure/volume overload; higher values generally mean more severe decompensation. Levels can also rise with renal dysfunction and are lower in obesity.

name: Central Venous Oxygen Saturation
shortExplanation: The oxygen saturation of blood returning through a central line, used as a marker of the balance between oxygen delivery and how much tissue is using.

sections.normalRange: Approximately 65-70% or higher for ScvO2 measured from a central venous catheter.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A low value suggests oxygen delivery is not keeping up with demand - from low cardiac output, anemia, hypoxemia, or increased consumption - as seen in shock. An unusually high value can reflect impaired oxygen extraction by tissues, as in some cases of septic shock. Trends help guide resuscitation.

name: Complete Blood Count (CBC)
shortExplanation: A common panel measuring the red cells, white cells, and platelets to screen for infection, anemia, and bleeding risk.

sections.normalRange: Includes white blood cells (about 4.5-11 x10^9/L), hemoglobin (about 12-16 g/dL in women and 13.5-17.5 in men), hematocrit, and platelets (about 150-400 x10^9/L).
sections.abnormalMeaning: A high white count suggests infection or inflammation and a low count suggests marrow suppression; low hemoglobin and hematocrit indicate anemia or blood loss; low platelets raise bleeding risk.

name: Creatinine
shortExplanation: A blood waste product filtered by the kidneys; it is the main marker used to track kidney function.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 0.6-1.2 mg/dL, varying with muscle mass, sex, and age.
sections.abnormalMeaning: A rising creatinine indicates worsening kidney function and is used to estimate the GFR for staging kidney disease. Low values usually reflect low muscle mass.

name: Digoxin Level
shortExplanation: A blood level checked to keep digoxin in its narrow safe range — too high risks toxicity and dangerous arrhythmias.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 0.5–2.0 ng/mL, with lower targets (about 0.5–0.9) often preferred in heart failure. Drawn at least 6 hours after the dose.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated levels (worsened by hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and renal impairment) point to toxicity — nausea, visual changes, and arrhythmias. Interpret alongside symptoms and potassium.

name: Glucose
shortExplanation: Blood sugar level — closely monitored in patients with diabetes, on insulin therapy, or during critical illness.

sections.normalRange: Roughly 70–100 mg/dL fasting; targets differ for hospitalized/critically ill patients and vary by institution protocol.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Low (hypoglycemia): shakiness, confusion, risk of loss of consciousness if severe. High (hyperglycemia): can indicate poor diabetes control or acute illness stress response; markedly elevated with ketosis suggests DKA.

name: Hemoglobin A1c
shortExplanation: A blood test that reflects average glucose control over the past two to three months, used to diagnose and monitor diabetes.

sections.normalRange: Below 5.7% is normal, 5.7-6.4% indicates prediabetes, and 6.5% or higher indicates diabetes.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Higher values reflect poorer average glucose control. A common target for many adults with diabetes is under about 7%, individualized to the patient.

name: INR
shortExplanation: A standardized measure of how long blood takes to clot — used to monitor and dose warfarin therapy.

sections.normalRange: About 0.8–1.1 without anticoagulation; therapeutic range on warfarin is usually 2.0–3.0 depending on indication.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Too low: inadequate anticoagulation, clot risk. Too high: bleeding risk — may require holding warfarin or reversal with vitamin K.

name: Lactate
shortExplanation: A blood marker that rises when tissues aren't getting enough oxygen — trended to gauge severity and response to treatment in sepsis and shock.

sections.normalRange: Typically <2 mmol/L.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated lactate suggests tissue hypoperfusion; a downward trend with treatment suggests improving perfusion, while a persistently high or rising lactate is a poor prognostic sign.

name: Lipid Panel
shortExplanation: A cholesterol blood test used to estimate cardiovascular risk and guide statin therapy — LDL is the main treatment target.

sections.normalRange: LDL is risk-dependent (often a goal <100 mg/dL, or <70 for high-risk patients); HDL >40–50 mg/dL; triglycerides <150 mg/dL.
sections.abnormalMeaning: High LDL and triglycerides with low HDL raise atherosclerotic risk; used to start or intensify statin therapy after events like ACS.

name: Lithium Level
shortExplanation: A blood test that measures the concentration of lithium to keep it in the effective range and avoid toxicity.

sections.normalRange: Maintenance therapeutic range is generally about 0.6-1.2 mEq/L, drawn as a trough roughly 12 hours after the last dose. Levels above about 1.5 mEq/L are considered toxic.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Low levels may mean the dose is inadequate or doses were missed. High levels signal toxicity, with rising severity from tremor and GI upset to confusion, ataxia, seizures, and coma. Dehydration, low sodium, kidney impairment, and drugs such as NSAIDs, thiazide diuretics, and ACE inhibitors can raise the level.

name: Magnesium
shortExplanation: An electrolyte essential for stable heart rhythm and muscle function — low levels raise the risk of dangerous arrhythmias.

sections.normalRange: About 1.7–2.2 mg/dL (varies by lab).
sections.abnormalMeaning: Low (hypomagnesemia): increases arrhythmia risk (including torsades de pointes) and worsens hypokalemia and digoxin toxicity. High (hypermagnesemia): can cause weakness, hypotension, and bradycardia.

name: Phosphate
shortExplanation: A blood mineral that becomes elevated in kidney failure and contributes to bone and mineral disease.

sections.normalRange: About 2.5-4.5 mg/dL.
sections.abnormalMeaning: High phosphate is common in kidney failure and contributes to bone and mineral disease and itching; low phosphate can occur with refeeding, malnutrition, or during treatment of DKA.

name: Potassium
shortExplanation: An electrolyte critical for heart and muscle function — closely monitored in patients on diuretics.

sections.abnormalMeaning: Low: muscle weakness, arrhythmia risk — common with loop diuretics. High: cardiac arrhythmia risk.

name: Procalcitonin
shortExplanation: A blood marker that tends to rise with serious bacterial infection, sometimes used to support decisions about starting or stopping antibiotics.

sections.normalRange: Typically low (often under about 0.1 ng/mL) in healthy people; interpretation depends on the clinical context and the lab's reference thresholds.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Higher levels are associated with bacterial infection and sepsis, and a falling trend can support de-escalating or stopping antibiotics. It is less elevated in most viral infections. It is an adjunct only and should never replace clinical judgment or cultures; it can rise in non-infectious conditions such as major trauma or surgery.

name: Troponin
shortExplanation: A protein released into the blood when heart muscle is damaged — the key lab value used to help diagnose a heart attack.

sections.normalRange: Typically <0.04 ng/mL, but the exact cutoff and assay type vary by lab — trended serially rather than interpreted from a single value.
sections.abnormalMeaning: Elevated and rising troponin suggests myocardial injury; the pattern of rise/fall over serial measurements helps distinguish acute injury from other causes of elevation (e.g. renal failure, sepsis).

name: Acetaminophen
shortExplanation: A common pain reliever and fever reducer that, unlike NSAIDs, has little anti-inflammatory effect and does not thin the blood or irritate the stomach.

sections.mechanism: Analgesic and antipyretic believed to act centrally; it does not meaningfully reduce inflammation or affect platelets.
sections.sideEffects: Generally well tolerated at recommended doses.
sections.adverseEffects: Liver injury (hepatotoxicity) in overdose or with chronic high doses, especially with alcohol use or existing liver disease.
sections.nursingImplications: Add up the total daily dose from all sources, including combination products, and stay within accepted daily limits (lower in liver disease). Acetylcysteine is the antidote for overdose.

name: Adenosine
shortExplanation: A very fast-acting drug that briefly "pauses" the heart to break certain rapid rhythms (SVT) and reset a normal beat.
