sections.mechanism: Transiently blocks AV node conduction, interrupting reentrant SVT. Extremely short half-life (seconds) — must be given as a rapid IV push followed immediately by a saline flush, ideally at a site close to the heart.
sections.sideEffects: Brief flushing, chest tightness, a sense of impending doom, a short sinus pause — all typically last seconds.
sections.adverseEffects: Transient asystole, bronchospasm in asthmatics, brief high-grade AV block.
sections.nursingImplications: Give as fast IV push with an immediate flush (two-syringe or stopcock technique); warn the patient about the brief uncomfortable feeling; have continuous ECG running and a defibrillator nearby.

name: Albuterol
shortExplanation: A fast-acting inhaled medication that opens the airways to make breathing easier — commonly used during a COPD or asthma flare.

sections.mechanism: Short-acting beta-2 agonist — relaxes bronchial smooth muscle. Onset within minutes, often given via nebulizer or inhaler during acute exacerbations.
sections.sideEffects: Tremor, tachycardia, nervousness.
sections.adverseEffects: Significant tachyarrhythmia in sensitive patients, hypokalemia with frequent dosing.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor heart rate, especially with frequent/repeated dosing; assess respiratory status before and after administration.

name: Alkylating Agents (class)
shortExplanation: A class of chemotherapy drugs, including cyclophosphamide, that damage cancer cell DNA so the cells cannot divide. They are used across many cancer types.

sections.mechanism: Attach alkyl groups to DNA, causing cross-links and strand breaks that prevent DNA replication and trigger cell death; they work regardless of cell cycle phase.
sections.sideEffects: Myelosuppression, nausea and vomiting, hair loss, and fatigue.
sections.adverseEffects: Hemorrhagic cystitis with cyclophosphamide and ifosfamide (mesna and hydration are protective), infertility, pulmonary fibrosis with some agents, and a long-term risk of secondary cancers.
sections.nursingImplications: Ensure adequate hydration and, with cyclophosphamide/ifosfamide, encourage frequent voiding and give mesna as ordered. Monitor blood counts, watch for infection and bleeding, and manage nausea with antiemetics.

name: Amiodarone
shortExplanation: An antiarrhythmic medication used to control or convert abnormal heart rhythms, most often atrial fibrillation.

sections.mechanism: Class III antiarrhythmic — prolongs the cardiac action potential, affecting multiple ion channels. Long half-life (weeks); IV loading followed by oral maintenance is common.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, photosensitivity, injection site phlebitis (IV).
sections.adverseEffects: Pulmonary toxicity, thyroid dysfunction (hyper- or hypothyroidism), liver toxicity, bradycardia/hypotension with IV administration.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor heart rate/rhythm and blood pressure during IV administration; monitor liver and thyroid function with long-term use.

name: Amoxicillin
shortExplanation: A penicillin-class antibiotic commonly used in children for ear infections, strep throat, and pneumonia.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis, killing susceptible bacteria.
sections.sideEffects: Diarrhea, nausea, and rash.
sections.adverseEffects: Allergic reactions ranging from hives to anaphylaxis in penicillin-allergic patients, and rarely severe skin reactions or C. difficile-associated diarrhea.
sections.nursingImplications: Dosing in children is weight-based; confirm the child has no penicillin allergy before giving. Encourage completing the full course, shake liquid suspensions well, and report any rash, which may signal allergy.

name: Apixaban
shortExplanation: An oral anticoagulant (DOAC) used to prevent strokes in atrial fibrillation and to treat clots — no routine INR monitoring needed, unlike warfarin.

sections.mechanism: Directly inhibits factor Xa. Predictable dosing without routine coagulation monitoring; shorter half-life than warfarin.
sections.sideEffects: Bruising, minor bleeding.
sections.adverseEffects: Major bleeding (GI, intracranial); reversal with andexanet alfa when available.
sections.nursingImplications: Reinforce not to skip doses (short half-life means clot risk returns quickly); assess for bleeding; note dose reductions for age, weight, and renal function; usually held before procedures per orders.

name: Aspirin
shortExplanation: An antiplatelet that makes platelets less sticky — given early in a suspected heart attack and taken long-term to prevent clots in the coronary arteries.

sections.mechanism: Irreversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX-1), blocking thromboxane A2 and reducing platelet aggregation for the life of the platelet. In suspected ACS, a non-enteric 162–325 mg tablet is chewed for rapid absorption.
sections.sideEffects: GI upset, easy bruising, minor bleeding.
sections.adverseEffects: GI bleeding/ulceration, allergic reaction/bronchospasm, Reye syndrome in children with viral illness.
sections.nursingImplications: Have the patient chew (don't swallow whole) in suspected MI for faster onset; assess for bleeding and GI symptoms; ask about aspirin allergy before giving.
sections.commonBrandName: Bayer, Ecotrin. Often written as ASA.

name: Atorvastatin
shortExplanation: A statin that lowers cholesterol — used to slow plaque buildup in arteries and reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic cholesterol synthesis, lowering LDL and stabilizing atherosclerotic plaque. High-intensity dosing is standard after ACS.
sections.sideEffects: Muscle aches, GI upset, headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Myopathy/rhabdomyolysis (muscle pain with dark urine), elevated liver enzymes.
sections.nursingImplications: Ask about new muscle pain or weakness; monitor liver function per orders; typically dosed in the evening; counsel to avoid large amounts of grapefruit juice.

name: Atropine
shortExplanation: Speeds up a dangerously slow heart rate by blocking the vagal "brake" on the heart — first-line drug for symptomatic bradycardia.

sections.mechanism: Anticholinergic — blocks muscarinic receptors, reducing vagal tone and increasing sinus node firing and AV conduction. ACLS dose is 1 mg IV every 3–5 minutes (max 3 mg) for symptomatic bradycardia.
sections.sideEffects: Dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, tachycardia, flushing.
sections.adverseEffects: Excessive tachycardia worsening myocardial ischemia; confusion/delirium especially in older adults; may be ineffective in high-grade (infranodal) heart block.
sections.nursingImplications: Push rapidly (slow push can paradoxically slow the heart); monitor rhythm and heart rate response; prepare transcutaneous pacing as a backup if atropine fails.

name: Betamethasone
shortExplanation: A corticosteroid given to the mother before an anticipated preterm birth to speed up the baby's lung development and reduce complications of prematurity.

sections.mechanism: Crosses the placenta and stimulates fetal surfactant production and lung maturation, lowering the risk of respiratory distress syndrome.
sections.sideEffects: Maternal elevated blood glucose, transient reduction in fetal movement, insomnia.
sections.adverseEffects: Worsened hyperglycemia in mothers with diabetes; potential immunosuppression with concurrent infection.
sections.nursingImplications: Given as a course of intramuscular injections spaced apart; the benefit builds over about 24-48 hours, so timing matters. Monitor maternal blood glucose, especially in diabetics, and continue to assess fetal well-being.

name: Caffeine Citrate
shortExplanation: A stimulant given to premature infants to reduce episodes of apnea by supporting their immature breathing control.

sections.mechanism: A methylxanthine that stimulates the central respiratory drive and increases sensitivity to carbon dioxide, reducing apnea episodes.
sections.sideEffects: Tachycardia, jitteriness, and feeding intolerance.
sections.adverseEffects: Signs of toxicity include marked tachycardia, agitation, and, rarely, seizures.
sections.nursingImplications: Usually given once daily with a loading dose followed by maintenance dosing. Monitor heart rate, for apnea frequency and response, and for feeding tolerance. It has a wide safety margin and long half-life in neonates, so routine level monitoring is often not required.

name: Calcium Gluconate
shortExplanation: An IV calcium salt used to protect the heart in hyperkalemia, to treat low calcium, and as the antidote for magnesium toxicity.

sections.mechanism: Raises extracellular calcium, which stabilizes cardiac cell membranes; in hyperkalemia it protects the heart but does not lower potassium.
sections.sideEffects: Warmth or flushing during infusion.
sections.adverseEffects: Bradycardia if pushed too fast and tissue injury with extravasation (less severe than calcium chloride).
sections.nursingImplications: Used for hyperkalemia with ECG changes, symptomatic low calcium, and magnesium toxicity. Monitor the ECG, give slowly, and ensure a patent IV.

name: Ceftriaxone
shortExplanation: A broad-spectrum injectable antibiotic used for many common infections, including pneumonia and urinary tract/kidney infections.

sections.mechanism: Third-generation cephalosporin that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis.
sections.sideEffects: Diarrhea, injection-site reactions, rash.
sections.adverseEffects: Allergic reactions (caution with penicillin allergy) and C. difficile infection. Avoid co-administration with calcium-containing IV fluids in neonates.
sections.nursingImplications: Assess allergy history before giving. Monitor for rash or anaphylaxis and for diarrhea suggesting C. difficile.

name: Cisplatin
shortExplanation: A platinum-based chemotherapy drug used for many solid tumors, including testicular, ovarian, bladder, and lung cancers. It is notable for kidney toxicity, severe nausea, and hearing loss.

sections.mechanism: A platinum compound that forms DNA cross-links, blocking DNA replication and transcription and triggering cancer cell death.
sections.sideEffects: Severe nausea and vomiting, myelosuppression, and fatigue.
sections.adverseEffects: Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity (hearing loss and tinnitus), peripheral neuropathy, and electrolyte wasting such as low magnesium.
sections.nursingImplications: Give aggressive IV hydration before and after the dose to protect the kidneys and monitor urine output, creatinine, and electrolytes (especially magnesium and potassium). Provide strong antiemetic prophylaxis, ask about hearing changes and numbness, and replace electrolytes as ordered.

name: Clopidogrel
shortExplanation: An antiplatelet often paired with aspirin (dual antiplatelet therapy) after a stent or heart attack to keep the coronary arteries from re-clotting.

sections.mechanism: Irreversibly blocks the platelet P2Y12 ADP receptor, inhibiting aggregation. A prodrug activated in the liver — effect is reduced in poor CYP2C19 metabolizers.
sections.sideEffects: Bruising, minor bleeding, GI upset.
sections.adverseEffects: Major bleeding; rarely thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP).
sections.nursingImplications: Emphasize adherence after coronary stenting (stopping early risks stent thrombosis); assess for bleeding; note it's usually held several days before surgery per orders.

name: Dantrolene
shortExplanation: A skeletal muscle relaxant that is the specific antidote for malignant hyperthermia. It stops the runaway muscle metabolism that drives the crisis.

sections.mechanism: Blocks the ryanodine receptor in skeletal muscle, reducing calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum so muscle contraction and the hypermetabolic state subside.
sections.sideEffects: Muscle weakness, drowsiness, dizziness, and phlebitis at the IV site.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory muscle weakness, hepatotoxicity with prolonged oral use, and tissue injury if it extravasates.
sections.nursingImplications: In an MH crisis, reconstitute and give rapidly; older formulations require vigorous shaking with many vials, while the concentrated formulation reconstitutes faster. Monitor muscle strength, respiratory status, temperature, and IV site, and continue dosing until the crisis resolves.

name: Dexmedetomidine
shortExplanation: An IV sedative that calms patients while keeping them relatively easy to arouse and without suppressing breathing, often used for light ICU sedation and to ease weaning from the ventilator.

sections.mechanism: Selective alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that reduces sympathetic outflow, producing sedation and analgesia with minimal respiratory depression.
sections.sideEffects: Bradycardia, hypotension, and dry mouth are common. A transient rise in blood pressure can occur with rapid loading.
sections.adverseEffects: Marked bradycardia and hypotension; rebound hypertension and agitation can follow abrupt discontinuation after prolonged use.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor heart rate and blood pressure closely. Because it does not blunt respiratory drive, it can be continued during ventilator weaning and extubation. Titrate to a sedation goal and taper rather than stopping abruptly after long infusions.

name: Digoxin
shortExplanation: Strengthens the heart's contraction and slows the heart rate — used in some heart failure and atrial fibrillation patients. Has a narrow safety margin.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits the Na-K-ATPase pump, increasing intracellular calcium (positive inotropy) and enhancing vagal tone to slow AV conduction. Narrow therapeutic index — levels and potassium matter.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, anorexia, visual changes (yellow-green halos), bradycardia.
sections.adverseEffects: Digoxin toxicity — worsened by hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and renal impairment — causing dangerous arrhythmias; reversed with digoxin immune Fab.
sections.nursingImplications: Check apical pulse for a full minute and hold for bradycardia (commonly <60) per parameters; monitor potassium, magnesium, and renal function; know signs of toxicity.

name: Diltiazem
shortExplanation: A calcium channel blocker used to slow a fast heart rate (e.g. in atrial fibrillation) and lower blood pressure.

sections.mechanism: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker — slows AV node conduction (rate control) and relaxes vascular smooth muscle. IV for acute rate control, PO for maintenance.
sections.sideEffects: Hypotension, bradycardia, peripheral edema, headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Symptomatic bradycardia or heart block; worsening heart failure in reduced ejection fraction; hypotension with IV use.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor heart rate and blood pressure closely during IV administration; avoid combining with IV beta-blockers (additive AV block); hold per bradycardia/hypotension parameters.

name: Dobutamine
shortExplanation: An inotrope that strengthens the heart's pumping — used when a weak heart can't maintain adequate output, as in cardiogenic shock or decompensated heart failure.

sections.mechanism: Primarily a beta-1 agonist — increases contractility and cardiac output with modest effect on systemic vascular resistance (can lower blood pressure via beta-2 vasodilation).
sections.sideEffects: Tachycardia, palpitations, mild blood pressure changes.
sections.adverseEffects: Tachyarrhythmias, increased myocardial oxygen demand and ischemia, hypotension.
sections.nursingImplications: Continuous ECG and blood pressure monitoring (ideally arterial line); titrate to hemodynamic goals; watch for arrhythmias and ischemic chest pain.

name: Doxorubicin
shortExplanation: An anthracycline chemotherapy drug used for many cancers, including breast cancer, lymphoma, and leukemia. It is known for cumulative heart toxicity and for turning the urine red.

sections.mechanism: Intercalates into DNA and inhibits topoisomerase II, and generates free radicals, blocking DNA and RNA synthesis in dividing cells.
sections.sideEffects: Myelosuppression, nausea and vomiting, hair loss, mucositis, and harmless red-orange discoloration of urine.
sections.adverseEffects: Dose-related cardiotoxicity that can lead to cardiomyopathy and heart failure, and severe tissue necrosis if it extravasates (it is a potent vesicant).
sections.nursingImplications: Track the lifetime cumulative dose and monitor cardiac function (for example ejection fraction). Give through a reliable, well-placed IV or central line, monitor the site constantly for extravasation, and reassure the patient about red urine. Report any signs of heart failure such as dyspnea or edema.

name: Enoxaparin
shortExplanation: A low-molecular-weight heparin injected under the skin to prevent and treat blood clots.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits clotting factor Xa, reducing clot formation.
sections.sideEffects: Bruising and irritation at the injection site.
sections.adverseEffects: Bleeding and, less often than with unfractionated heparin, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia; it accumulates in kidney impairment.
sections.nursingImplications: Give subcutaneously (often the abdomen); do not expel the air bubble in the prefilled syringe and do not rub the site. Monitor platelets and for bleeding. Dose is reduced or avoided in severe renal impairment; anti-Xa levels are used when monitoring is needed.

name: Epinephrine
shortExplanation: A powerful medication that stimulates the heart and blood vessels — a cornerstone drug in cardiac arrest and anaphylaxis.

sections.mechanism: Alpha- and beta-adrenergic agonist — increases heart rate, contractility, and systemic vascular resistance. In cardiac arrest, 1 mg IV/IO every 3–5 minutes per ACLS.
sections.sideEffects: Tachycardia, palpitations, anxiety, tremor, hypertension.
sections.adverseEffects: Tachyarrhythmias, severe hypertension, myocardial ischemia; tissue necrosis with extravasation of concentrated infusions.
sections.nursingImplications: Know the concentration and route — arrest dosing (1 mg of 1:10,000 IV) differs sharply from anaphylaxis dosing (IM); double-check the code-cart dose; monitor rhythm and blood pressure continuously.

name: Epoetin Alfa
shortExplanation: A synthetic form of erythropoietin that stimulates the bone marrow to make red blood cells, used for anemia of chronic kidney disease.

sections.mechanism: An erythropoiesis-stimulating agent (ESA) that signals the marrow to produce red blood cells.
sections.sideEffects: Elevated blood pressure, injection-site reactions.
sections.adverseEffects: Worsening hypertension, clotting events (stroke, MI, clots), and higher cardiovascular risk if hemoglobin is raised too high or too quickly.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor hemoglobin and blood pressure. Ensure adequate iron stores for the drug to work. Target a conservative hemoglobin rather than a normal level.

name: Fentanyl
shortExplanation: A potent, fast-acting IV opioid used for pain control and sedation in critically ill and post-operative patients and during intubation.

sections.mechanism: Binds mu-opioid receptors to block pain signaling and blunt the stress response. Rapid onset and short duration when given as a single dose, but it accumulates with prolonged infusion.
sections.sideEffects: Sedation, respiratory depression, bradycardia, hypotension, constipation, nausea, and pruritus.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory depression and apnea; chest-wall rigidity with rapid high-dose IV push; tolerance and dependence with prolonged infusion.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor respiratory rate, sedation level, and oxygenation. Keep naloxone available for reversal. Pair analgesia with sedation goals (analgesia-first sedation). Anticipate withdrawal and titrate down after long infusions.

name: Filgrastim
shortExplanation: A granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF) that stimulates the bone marrow to make more neutrophils. It is used to shorten neutropenia and lower infection risk after chemotherapy.

sections.mechanism: A recombinant form of G-CSF that stimulates the production, maturation, and release of neutrophils from the bone marrow.
sections.sideEffects: Bone and muscle pain (often in the back and long bones), low-grade fever, and injection-site reactions.
sections.adverseEffects: Splenic enlargement or rare rupture, allergic reactions, and (uncommonly) acute respiratory distress or capillary leak.
sections.nursingImplications: Given by subcutaneous injection or IV, usually starting after chemotherapy and stopped before the next cycle. Monitor blood counts, manage bone pain with analgesics as needed, and report severe left-upper-abdominal or shoulder-tip pain (possible splenic issue) or breathing difficulty. It should not be given close to the time chemotherapy is administered.

name: Flumazenil
shortExplanation: The reversal drug for benzodiazepines, used in select cases of oversedation. It is given cautiously because it can trigger seizures.

sections.mechanism: Competitive antagonist at the benzodiazepine site on the GABA-A receptor, reversing benzodiazepine sedation and respiratory depression.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, dizziness, agitation, and flushing.
sections.adverseEffects: Seizures, especially in benzodiazepine-dependent patients or mixed overdoses with pro-convulsant drugs; resedation when the benzodiazepine outlasts flumazenil.
sections.nursingImplications: Avoid in patients on chronic benzodiazepines or with suspected tricyclic co-ingestion because of seizure risk. Support airway and breathing first. Monitor for resedation because it is short-acting and redosing may be required.

name: Furosemide
shortExplanation: Helps the body get rid of extra fluid by making the kidneys release more sodium and water — commonly used when fluid buildup makes it hard to breathe or puts strain on the heart.

sections.mechanism: Loop diuretic — inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the loop of Henle. Watch for hypokalemia, hypotension, and ototoxicity with rapid IV push.
sections.sideEffects: Increased urination, dehydration, low potassium (hypokalemia), dizziness or low blood pressure.
sections.adverseEffects: Hearing changes or ringing in the ears (ototoxicity) with rapid IV push; severe electrolyte imbalance; allergic reaction in patients with sulfa sensitivity.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor potassium and renal function, watch for orthostatic hypotension, track daily weights and I&Os.
sections.commonBrandName: Lasix. Usually given IV push or PO depending on acuity.

name: Gabapentin
shortExplanation: A medication for nerve (neuropathic) pain and seizures, often used as part of multimodal pain control.

sections.mechanism: Modulates voltage-gated calcium channels, dampening abnormal nerve signaling.
sections.sideEffects: Dizziness, drowsiness, unsteadiness, peripheral edema.
sections.adverseEffects: Excess sedation and respiratory depression when combined with opioids or other CNS depressants; accumulates in kidney impairment.
sections.nursingImplications: Renally cleared, so the dose is reduced in kidney disease. Monitor sedation, especially with opioids. Do not stop abruptly; taper to avoid withdrawal.

name: Haloperidol
shortExplanation: A first-generation (typical) antipsychotic used for psychosis and severe agitation.

sections.mechanism: Blocks dopamine D2 receptors in the brain, reducing psychotic symptoms and agitation.
sections.sideEffects: Sedation, restlessness (akathisia), and dry mouth.
sections.adverseEffects: Extrapyramidal symptoms including acute dystonia, parkinsonism, and tardive dyskinesia; QT prolongation; and neuroleptic malignant syndrome, a rare but life-threatening reaction.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor for muscle stiffness, abnormal movements, and restlessness, and for signs of neuroleptic malignant syndrome such as high fever and rigidity. Obtain an ECG when high doses or IV use raise QT concerns. Anticholinergic medications can treat acute dystonic reactions.

name: Heparin
shortExplanation: An anticoagulant that prevents blood clots from forming or growing larger — used for DVT/PE treatment and prevention.

sections.mechanism: Potentiates antithrombin III, inactivating thrombin and factor Xa. IV (unfractionated) requires continuous infusion with frequent aPTT monitoring; subcutaneous dosing used for prophylaxis.
sections.sideEffects: Bruising, bleeding, injection site irritation (subQ).
sections.adverseEffects: Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) — a serious immune reaction; major bleeding, especially with supratherapeutic aPTT.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor aPTT (IV) or anti-Xa levels, platelet counts (watch for HIT), signs of bleeding. Have protamine sulfate available as reversal agent.

name: Hydromorphone
shortExplanation: A potent opioid for severe pain; because it is stronger than morphine by weight, small dosing errors can cause serious harm.

sections.mechanism: Agonist at mu opioid receptors; more potent than morphine on a milligram basis.
sections.sideEffects: Sedation, constipation, nausea, itching.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory depression, low blood pressure, and dependence.
sections.nursingImplications: A high-alert medication: verify the dose carefully and do not confuse with morphine. Monitor respiratory rate and sedation closely; keep naloxone available; start a bowel regimen.

name: Hypertonic Saline
shortExplanation: Concentrated salt solution (such as 3%) given IV to reduce brain swelling and treat dangerously low sodium.

sections.mechanism: Raises blood osmolality and sodium, drawing water out of swollen brain tissue to lower intracranial pressure; also corrects symptomatic hyponatremia.
sections.sideEffects: Thirst, elevated sodium, and fluid overload.
sections.adverseEffects: Overly rapid sodium correction can cause osmotic demyelination; fluid overload and pulmonary edema; phlebitis or tissue injury with peripheral extravasation of higher concentrations.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor serum sodium frequently and correct at a controlled rate to avoid overcorrection. Higher concentrations are usually given through a central line. Watch neuro status, volume status, and the IV site closely.

name: Ibuprofen
shortExplanation: A nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used for pain, inflammation, and fever.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits COX enzymes, lowering prostaglandins to reduce pain, inflammation, and fever.
sections.sideEffects: Stomach upset, dyspepsia, heartburn.
sections.adverseEffects: GI bleeding and ulcers, kidney injury (especially with dehydration or existing kidney disease), fluid retention and raised blood pressure, and increased cardiovascular risk.
sections.nursingImplications: Give with food. Use cautiously or avoid in kidney disease, heart failure, GI bleed risk, and older adults. Monitor renal function and watch for signs of GI bleeding.

name: Insulin
shortExplanation: A hormone that lowers blood glucose by helping cells absorb sugar from the blood — used to manage diabetes and to treat diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).

sections.mechanism: Rapid-acting forms (e.g. lispro) peak quickly and are short-lived; long-acting forms (e.g. glargine) give steady basal coverage. IV regular insulin is used in DKA for rapid, titratable effect.
sections.sideEffects: Hypoglycemia, injection site reactions, weight gain.
sections.adverseEffects: Severe hypoglycemia (confusion, seizure, loss of consciousness); hypokalemia with IV insulin therapy (drives potassium intracellularly).
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor blood glucose closely, especially with IV infusions; monitor potassium during DKA treatment; know the onset/peak/duration of the specific formulation in use.

name: Ketamine
shortExplanation: A dissociative anesthetic used for sedation, induction during intubation, procedural sedation, and analgesia, notable for preserving airway reflexes and blood pressure.

sections.mechanism: Blocks NMDA receptors to produce a dissociative, trance-like state with analgesia and amnesia. Stimulates the sympathetic system, which tends to support blood pressure and heart rate.
sections.sideEffects: Increased blood pressure and heart rate, increased secretions, nystagmus, and emergence reactions (vivid dreams, hallucinations) on waking.
sections.adverseEffects: Emergence delirium, laryngospasm (especially with copious secretions), and hypertension/tachycardia that may be undesirable in some patients.
sections.nursingImplications: Useful for induction in hypotensive or bronchospastic patients because it supports hemodynamics and bronchodilates. Provide a calm, low-stimulation recovery to limit emergence reactions. Monitor airway, secretions, and blood pressure.

name: Levofloxacin
shortExplanation: A fluoroquinolone antibiotic used for respiratory and urinary infections when broad coverage is needed.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits bacterial DNA enzymes (gyrase/topoisomerase) needed for DNA replication.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, headache, diarrhea.
sections.adverseEffects: Boxed warnings for tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, and CNS effects; also QT prolongation, blood glucose swings, and C. difficile.
sections.nursingImplications: Separate dosing from antacids, iron, and calcium, which impair absorption. Monitor glucose in patients with diabetes and watch for new tendon or joint pain and confusion.

name: Lisinopril
shortExplanation: Relaxes blood vessels to lower blood pressure and take pressure off the heart.

sections.mechanism: ACE inhibitor — blocks conversion of angiotensin I to II.
sections.sideEffects: Dry cough, dizziness, elevated potassium.
sections.adverseEffects: Angioedema (rare but serious), hyperkalemia, acute kidney injury in volume-depleted patients.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor blood pressure and potassium; watch for signs of angioedema.

name: Lithium
shortExplanation: A mood stabilizer used to treat and prevent episodes of mania in bipolar disorder.

sections.mechanism: Its exact action is not fully understood, but it modulates neurotransmission and intracellular signaling to stabilize mood.
sections.sideEffects: Fine hand tremor, increased thirst and urination, weight gain, nausea, and mild cognitive dulling.
sections.adverseEffects: A narrow therapeutic window means toxicity can occur with small increases in level: coarse tremor, vomiting, diarrhea, confusion, ataxia, slurred speech, seizures, and coma. Long-term use can cause hypothyroidism and kidney impairment, and it is teratogenic.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor lithium levels along with kidney and thyroid function. Maintain steady salt and fluid intake, since dehydration, low sodium, and certain drugs (NSAIDs, some diuretics, ACE inhibitors) raise levels. Teach patients to recognize early signs of toxicity.

name: Loop Diuretics (class)
shortExplanation: The drug class furosemide belongs to — more potent than thiazide diuretics.

sections.mechanism: Act on the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle rather than the distal tubule, producing a stronger diuretic effect.
sections.sideEffects: Electrolyte depletion (potassium, magnesium, sodium), dehydration.
sections.adverseEffects: Ototoxicity with rapid IV administration, especially at high doses.

name: Lorazepam
shortExplanation: A benzodiazepine used for anxiety, agitation, seizures, and alcohol withdrawal.

sections.mechanism: Enhances the effect of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA, producing calming, sedative, and anticonvulsant effects.
sections.sideEffects: Drowsiness, dizziness, unsteadiness, and confusion.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory depression, especially when combined with opioids or alcohol, and physical dependence with tolerance and withdrawal after prolonged use. Paradoxical agitation can occur.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor level of consciousness and respiratory status, particularly with IV use or opioid co-administration. Use fall precautions. Flumazenil can reverse benzodiazepines but is used cautiously because it may precipitate seizures. Avoid abrupt discontinuation after prolonged use.

name: Magnesium Sulfate
shortExplanation: An electrolyte given IV to prevent seizures in severe preeclampsia and eclampsia, and used in obstetrics for fetal neuroprotection and short-term slowing of preterm labor.

sections.mechanism: Central nervous system depressant and smooth-muscle relaxant that raises the seizure threshold and reduces vascular and uterine tone.
sections.sideEffects: Flushing, warmth, nausea, drowsiness, blurred vision.
sections.adverseEffects: Magnesium toxicity progresses from loss of deep tendon reflexes to respiratory depression, hypotension, and cardiac arrest as levels rise.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor deep tendon reflexes, respiratory rate, level of consciousness, and urine output during infusion, since magnesium is renally cleared. Loss of reflexes is an early warning of toxicity. Keep calcium gluconate available as the antidote.

name: Mannitol
shortExplanation: An osmotic diuretic given IV to reduce elevated intracranial pressure and brain swelling by pulling fluid out of tissue and increasing urine output.

sections.mechanism: An osmotically active sugar that raises blood osmolality, drawing water out of brain tissue and into the bloodstream, then is excreted by the kidneys, producing diuresis.
sections.sideEffects: Large urine output, thirst, and electrolyte shifts.
sections.adverseEffects: Dehydration and hypotension from brisk diuresis, electrolyte disturbances, and acute kidney injury; rebound rise in intracranial pressure is possible.
sections.nursingImplications: Administer through an in-line filter because it can crystallize. Monitor serum osmolality (and the osmolar gap), electrolytes, kidney function, and strict intake and output. Watch neuro status and hold or reassess if the patient becomes hypotensive or oliguric.

name: Metformin
shortExplanation: A first-line oral medication for type 2 diabetes that lowers blood glucose and does not by itself cause hypoglycemia.

sections.mechanism: Reduces glucose production by the liver and improves the body's sensitivity to insulin.
sections.sideEffects: GI upset, diarrhea, metallic taste.
sections.adverseEffects: Rare lactic acidosis, especially with kidney impairment, low oxygen states, or after iodinated contrast; vitamin B12 deficiency with long-term use.
sections.nursingImplications: Often held around iodinated contrast and in acute kidney injury. Assess kidney function and take with food to reduce GI effects.

name: Methylergonovine
shortExplanation: An ergot medication used after delivery to firm up the uterus and control postpartum hemorrhage caused by uterine atony.

sections.mechanism: Directly stimulates sustained uterine smooth-muscle contraction, clamping down on bleeding vessels at the placental site.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, vomiting, cramping, headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Causes vasoconstriction and can trigger severe hypertension; it is contraindicated in preeclampsia and pre-existing hypertension. Rapid IV administration risks dangerous blood pressure spikes and is avoided.
sections.nursingImplications: Usually given intramuscularly for postpartum bleeding. Check blood pressure before and after administration and hold the dose if the patient is hypertensive. Assess uterine tone and lochia for response.

name: Metoprolol
shortExplanation: Slows and steadies the heartbeat so the heart doesn't have to work as hard.

sections.mechanism: Beta-1 selective blocker — reduces heart rate and myocardial oxygen demand.
sections.sideEffects: Fatigue, dizziness, cold extremities, slowed heart rate.
sections.adverseEffects: Symptomatic bradycardia, heart block, bronchospasm in susceptible patients.
sections.nursingImplications: Check apical pulse and blood pressure before administration.

name: Metronidazole
shortExplanation: An antibiotic that covers anaerobic bacteria and some protozoa, used for abdominal, pelvic, and certain intestinal infections.

sections.mechanism: Enters microbes and damages their DNA, killing anaerobic bacteria and protozoa.
sections.sideEffects: Metallic taste, nausea, headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Peripheral neuropathy with prolonged use and a disulfiram-like reaction (flushing, vomiting) with alcohol.
sections.nursingImplications: Advise avoiding alcohol during treatment and for a few days after. Used for intra-abdominal, anaerobic, and some C. difficile infections.

name: Midazolam
shortExplanation: A short-acting IV benzodiazepine used for sedation, anxiety and agitation, seizures, and as part of intubation.

sections.mechanism: Enhances GABA-A receptor activity, producing sedation, anxiolysis, amnesia, and anticonvulsant effects.
sections.sideEffects: Sedation, respiratory depression, hypotension, and anterograde amnesia.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory depression and apnea, especially when combined with opioids. Prolonged infusions accumulate and can delay awakening; abrupt withdrawal after long use can cause agitation and seizures.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor airway, respiratory rate, and oxygenation. Have flumazenil available as the reversal agent, though it is used cautiously. Combine cautiously with opioids because of additive respiratory depression.

name: Misoprostol
shortExplanation: A prostaglandin used in obstetrics to ripen the cervix and induce labor, and to contract the uterus in postpartum hemorrhage.

sections.mechanism: A prostaglandin E1 analog that softens and dilates the cervix and stimulates uterine contractions.
sections.sideEffects: Fever, chills, shivering, nausea, and diarrhea are common.
sections.adverseEffects: Uterine tachysystole with fetal heart rate changes and, rarely, uterine rupture, especially with a prior uterine scar.
sections.nursingImplications: Route and use depend on indication (cervical ripening versus postpartum bleeding). When used for induction, monitor contraction pattern and fetal heart rate closely. Fever and shaking after a postpartum dose are expected side effects rather than infection.

name: Morphine
shortExplanation: A strong opioid used for moderate to severe pain and, at times, for the breathlessness of heart failure.

sections.mechanism: Agonist at mu opioid receptors that reduces pain perception; also dilates veins.
sections.sideEffects: Sedation, constipation, nausea, itching, urinary retention.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory depression, low blood pressure, and dependence; risk rises when combined with other CNS depressants.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor respiratory rate, sedation level, and pain; hold and reassess if oversedated. Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity. Start a bowel regimen. Use caution in kidney impairment, where active metabolites accumulate.

name: Naloxone
shortExplanation: The reversal drug for opioid overdose that rapidly restores breathing by displacing opioids from their receptors.

sections.mechanism: Competitive opioid receptor antagonist that quickly reverses opioid-induced respiratory depression and sedation.
sections.sideEffects: Acute opioid withdrawal in dependent patients: agitation, sweating, nausea, tachycardia, and hypertension.
sections.adverseEffects: Precipitated withdrawal, rare pulmonary edema, and re-narcotization when the opioid outlasts naloxone, causing sedation and apnea to return.
sections.nursingImplications: Support airway and breathing first. Titrate to restore adequate respirations rather than full arousal to limit withdrawal. Because many opioids last longer than naloxone, keep monitoring and be ready to redose; repeat doses or an infusion may be needed.

name: Neostigmine
shortExplanation: A cholinesterase inhibitor used to reverse non-depolarizing muscle relaxants at the end of surgery. It is given with an anticholinergic to blunt its slowing effect on the heart.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits acetylcholinesterase, increasing acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction so it can outcompete residual non-depolarizing blocker and restore muscle strength.
sections.sideEffects: Bradycardia, increased salivation and secretions, nausea, and abdominal cramping.
sections.adverseEffects: Profound bradycardia, bronchospasm, and recurarization (residual weakness) if reversal is incomplete.
sections.nursingImplications: Usually given with glycopyrrolate or atropine to prevent bradycardia. Monitor heart rate, respiratory effort, and evidence of adequate reversal such as sustained head lift and strong grip before extubation.

name: Nitroglycerin
shortExplanation: A vasodilator that relieves chest pain (angina) by widening blood vessels and reducing the heart's workload.

sections.mechanism: Releases nitric oxide, relaxing vascular smooth muscle — venodilation lowers preload (the main effect) with some coronary vasodilation. Available sublingual, IV, and topical.
sections.sideEffects: Headache, flushing, dizziness, hypotension.
sections.adverseEffects: Severe hypotension, especially with volume depletion, right-ventricular/inferior MI, or recent PDE-5 inhibitor (e.g. sildenafil) use — a dangerous interaction.
sections.nursingImplications: Check blood pressure before and after each dose; sublingual angina dosing is one tab every 5 minutes up to 3 doses — call for help if pain persists; titrate IV to pain and BP.
sections.commonBrandName: Nitrostat, Nitro-Dur. Often called NTG or "nitro."

name: Norepinephrine
shortExplanation: A medication that raises blood pressure by tightening blood vessels — used when fluids alone aren't maintaining adequate blood pressure, especially in septic shock.

sections.mechanism: Potent alpha-1 agonist (with some beta-1 activity) causing vasoconstriction and increased cardiac contractility. First-line vasopressor in septic shock.
sections.sideEffects: Reflex bradycardia, headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Peripheral/digital ischemia with prolonged or high-dose use, especially with extravasation — should be given via central line when possible; arrhythmia.
sections.nursingImplications: Continuous BP monitoring, ideally via arterial line; assess extremities/IV site for signs of extravasation; titrate to MAP goal per orders.

name: Olanzapine
shortExplanation: A second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic used for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and acute agitation.

sections.mechanism: Blocks dopamine and serotonin receptors, improving psychotic and mood symptoms.
sections.sideEffects: Sedation, weight gain, increased appetite, and dizziness.
sections.adverseEffects: Metabolic effects including significant weight gain, high blood sugar, and abnormal lipids; neuroleptic malignant syndrome; and lower risk of movement disorders than typical antipsychotics. Combining intramuscular olanzapine with benzodiazepines has been linked to excessive sedation and cardiorespiratory depression.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor weight, blood glucose, and lipids over time. Watch for oversedation, and use caution about pairing the IM form closely with parenteral benzodiazepines. Assess for movement disorders and signs of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

name: Ondansetron
shortExplanation: A widely used anti-nausea medication that prevents and treats nausea and vomiting.

sections.mechanism: Blocks 5-HT3 serotonin receptors in the gut and brainstem that trigger nausea and vomiting.
sections.sideEffects: Headache, constipation, fatigue.
sections.adverseEffects: QT prolongation, which can lead to arrhythmias, particularly with other QT-prolonging drugs or electrolyte abnormalities.
sections.nursingImplications: Assess for nausea and response. Use caution with other QT-prolonging medications and check potassium/magnesium. Not effective for motion sickness.

name: Oxycodone
shortExplanation: An oral opioid for moderate to severe pain, often given as a combination product with acetaminophen.

sections.mechanism: Agonist at mu opioid receptors that reduces pain perception.
sections.sideEffects: Sedation, constipation, nausea, itching.
sections.adverseEffects: Respiratory depression, low blood pressure, and dependence, especially with other CNS depressants.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor sedation and respiratory rate; start a bowel regimen; naloxone reverses toxicity. Combination products (such as Percocet) contain acetaminophen, so track total daily acetaminophen. Extended-release forms are not to be crushed.

name: Oxytocin
shortExplanation: A hormone given IV to start or strengthen labor contractions and, after delivery, to contract the uterus and control bleeding.

sections.mechanism: Stimulates uterine smooth muscle to contract by increasing intracellular calcium; also promotes milk letdown.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, and with strong contractions, maternal discomfort.
sections.adverseEffects: Uterine tachysystole (too-frequent contractions) causing fetal heart rate decelerations and distress; uterine rupture; and, at high sustained doses, water intoxication/hyponatremia from its antidiuretic effect. Rapid IV bolus can cause hypotension.
sections.nursingImplications: Given by controlled infusion pump and titrated to contraction pattern. Continuously monitor contraction frequency and fetal heart rate; stop the infusion and reposition/give oxygen if tachysystole or a nonreassuring tracing develops. Track intake/output and watch for signs of fluid overload during prolonged infusions.

name: Pantoprazole
shortExplanation: A proton pump inhibitor (PPI) that reduces stomach acid, used for reflux, ulcers, and GI bleeding.

sections.mechanism: Blocks the stomach's acid (proton) pump, markedly reducing gastric acid production.
sections.sideEffects: Headache, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort.
sections.adverseEffects: Long-term use is associated with low magnesium, vitamin B12 deficiency, C. difficile infection, and bone fractures.
sections.nursingImplications: Give oral doses before meals. IV infusions are used in acute GI bleeding. Reassess ongoing need to avoid unnecessary long-term use.

name: Phenylephrine
shortExplanation: A vasopressor that raises blood pressure by tightening blood vessels, commonly used for hypotension in the PACU and OR and for anesthesia-related low blood pressure.

sections.mechanism: Selective alpha-1 adrenergic agonist that constricts blood vessels to raise systemic vascular resistance and blood pressure. A reflex slowing of the heart rate can occur.
sections.sideEffects: Reflex bradycardia, hypertension, and headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Severe hypertension, reflex bradycardia, and reduced organ perfusion or extravasation tissue injury if it leaks from the IV site.
sections.nursingImplications: Preferred when hypotension is paired with tachycardia because it does not increase heart rate. Monitor blood pressure and heart rate continuously, ideally with an arterial line for infusions, and give through a secure, well-monitored IV or central line per policy.

name: Piperacillin-Tazobactam
shortExplanation: A broad-spectrum IV antibiotic combination used empirically for serious infections and sepsis, covering many gram-positive, gram-negative, and anaerobic bacteria.

sections.mechanism: Piperacillin is a penicillin that disrupts bacterial cell wall synthesis; tazobactam is a beta-lactamase inhibitor that protects piperacillin from bacterial enzymes, broadening coverage.
sections.sideEffects: Diarrhea, nausea, rash, and headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Allergic and anaphylactic reactions (penicillin class), Clostridioides difficile colitis, and a risk of acute kidney injury when combined with vancomycin.
sections.nursingImplications: Screen for penicillin allergy. Often given as an extended infusion for better effect. Draw cultures before the first dose when possible and give antibiotics promptly in sepsis. Monitor renal function, especially when co-administered with vancomycin.

name: Potassium Chloride
shortExplanation: Furosemide causes the body to lose potassium along with fluid, so this tops it back up to a safe level.

sections.mechanism: Electrolyte replacement. IV formulations must always be diluted and infused at a controlled rate.
sections.sideEffects: GI upset (oral form), infusion site discomfort (IV form).
sections.adverseEffects: Cardiac arrhythmia if infused too quickly or given undiluted IV.
sections.nursingImplications: Verify potassium level and renal function before administering.

name: Prednisone
shortExplanation: An oral corticosteroid used to reduce inflammation and calm the immune system in many conditions, including COPD and asthma flares.

sections.mechanism: A glucocorticoid that broadly suppresses inflammation and immune activity.
sections.sideEffects: Increased appetite, insomnia, mood changes, fluid retention, elevated blood glucose.
sections.adverseEffects: With prolonged use: high blood sugar, infection risk, osteoporosis, adrenal suppression, GI ulcers, and muscle wasting.
sections.nursingImplications: Give with food. Do not stop abruptly after prolonged use; taper as ordered. Monitor blood glucose and for signs of infection.

name: Propofol
shortExplanation: A fast-acting IV sedative-hypnotic used for procedural sedation, induction of anesthesia, and continuous sedation of intubated patients.

sections.mechanism: Enhances inhibitory GABA-A receptor activity in the brain, producing rapid sedation and hypnosis. Very short-acting, so sedation deepens or lightens quickly when the infusion rate changes.
sections.sideEffects: Dose-dependent hypotension, respiratory depression, apnea, pain at the injection site, and green-tinged urine.
sections.adverseEffects: Propofol infusion syndrome (rare but often fatal) with prolonged high-dose use: metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, and cardiac failure. Formulated in a lipid emulsion, so it adds calories and can raise triglycerides.
sections.nursingImplications: Requires continuous cardiorespiratory monitoring and airway support. Titrate to a sedation goal (RASS). Change the bottle and tubing per protocol (usually every 12 hours) because the lipid emulsion supports bacterial growth. Monitor triglycerides on prolonged infusions.

name: Racemic Epinephrine
shortExplanation: A nebulized form of epinephrine used to quickly shrink swollen upper airway tissues in children with croup or stridor.

sections.mechanism: Stimulates alpha-adrenergic receptors to constrict blood vessels in the airway mucosa, reducing swelling and easing airflow.
sections.sideEffects: Transient tachycardia, tremor, pallor, and jitteriness.
sections.adverseEffects: Rebound airway swelling can occur as the drug wears off, so children need observation after treatment before discharge.
sections.nursingImplications: Given by nebulizer for moderate to severe stridor. Monitor heart rate, respiratory effort, and oxygen saturation, and observe the child for a period after administration to watch for return of stridor.

name: Rho(D) Immune Globulin
shortExplanation: An injection given to Rh-negative mothers to prevent their immune system from making antibodies against an Rh-positive baby's blood, which protects future pregnancies.

sections.mechanism: Provides passive anti-D antibodies that bind and clear any Rh-positive fetal red cells before the mother's immune system is sensitized to them.
sections.sideEffects: Soreness at the injection site, low-grade fever.
sections.adverseEffects: Allergic/hypersensitivity reactions are uncommon.
sections.nursingImplications: Typically given intramuscularly around 28 weeks and again within 72 hours after delivery if the newborn is Rh-positive, and after events like miscarriage, amniocentesis, or trauma. Verify maternal Rh-negative status and antibody screen before giving. It prevents sensitization but does not treat existing antibodies.

name: Risperidone
shortExplanation: A second-generation (atypical) antipsychotic used for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and irritability associated with autism.

sections.mechanism: Blocks dopamine and serotonin receptors to reduce psychotic and mood symptoms.
sections.sideEffects: Sedation, weight gain, dizziness, and increased prolactin, which can cause breast changes or menstrual irregularities.
sections.adverseEffects: Higher rates of extrapyramidal symptoms and prolactin elevation than some other atypicals, metabolic changes, and neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor for movement disorders, orthostatic hypotension, weight, glucose, and lipids, and ask about prolactin-related symptoms. A long-acting injectable form exists for adherence. Assess for signs of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

name: Rocuronium
shortExplanation: A non-depolarizing paralytic that relaxes skeletal muscle to enable intubation and mechanical ventilation. It does not provide any sedation or pain relief.

sections.mechanism: Competitively blocks acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, preventing muscle contraction. Rapid onset makes it a common choice for rapid sequence intubation.
sections.sideEffects: Prolonged paralysis if metabolism is impaired; injection-site discomfort.
sections.adverseEffects: Complete inability to breathe or move while the drug is active - the patient must be ventilated. Awareness with paralysis if sedation and analgesia are inadequate; rare anaphylaxis.
sections.nursingImplications: Never give without adequate sedation and analgesia - the patient can be fully aware but unable to move. Ensure the airway is secured and ventilation is controlled. Sugammadex reverses rocuronium; monitor recovery with a train-of-four nerve stimulator.

name: Scopolamine
shortExplanation: An anticholinergic drug used to dry up excess secretions and to prevent nausea and motion sickness. In hospice it is often used to reduce noisy respiratory secretions (the death rattle) near the end of life.

sections.mechanism: Blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, reducing secretions from salivary and respiratory glands and dampening the nausea and vomiting pathways.
sections.sideEffects: Dry mouth, blurred vision, drowsiness, urinary retention, and constipation.
sections.adverseEffects: Confusion, delirium, and agitation (especially in older adults), tachycardia, and worsening of narrow-angle glaucoma.
sections.nursingImplications: Available as a transdermal patch and other forms. For end-of-life secretions, combine with repositioning and reassure the family that the sound is usually not distressing to the patient. Monitor for anticholinergic effects such as confusion and urinary retention, and keep the patch away from the eyes (wash hands after handling).

name: Sertraline
shortExplanation: A selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) used to treat depression and various anxiety disorders.

sections.mechanism: Blocks reuptake of serotonin in the brain, increasing its availability to improve mood and anxiety over time.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, diarrhea, headache, insomnia or drowsiness, and sexual dysfunction; gastrointestinal effects often ease after the first weeks.
sections.adverseEffects: Serotonin syndrome when combined with other serotonergic drugs, increased bleeding risk, hyponatremia, and a boxed warning for increased suicidal thinking in children, adolescents, and young adults early in treatment.
sections.nursingImplications: Teach that full benefit takes several weeks, so adherence matters. Monitor mood and for emerging suicidal thoughts, especially early on. Do not stop abruptly to avoid discontinuation symptoms, and review other medications for serotonergic interactions.

name: Sevelamer
shortExplanation: A phosphate binder taken with meals to lower high phosphate levels in chronic kidney disease and dialysis patients.

sections.mechanism: A non-calcium binder that traps dietary phosphate in the gut so it passes in the stool rather than being absorbed.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, bloating, constipation or diarrhea.
sections.adverseEffects: GI intolerance; rare bowel obstruction with prior GI motility problems.
sections.nursingImplications: Must be taken with meals to work. Separate from certain other oral medications. Monitor phosphate and calcium levels.

name: Sevoflurane
shortExplanation: An inhaled volatile anesthetic used to induce and maintain general anesthesia. It is well tolerated for mask induction, especially in children.

sections.mechanism: A halogenated volatile agent that enhances inhibitory neurotransmission (largely GABA-A) in the central nervous system to produce unconsciousness and amnesia; dose is titrated by inhaled concentration.
sections.sideEffects: Hypotension, respiratory depression, and postoperative nausea and vomiting; emergence agitation, particularly in children.
sections.adverseEffects: A known trigger of malignant hyperthermia in susceptible patients; dose-dependent cardiorespiratory depression.
sections.nursingImplications: Delivered by the anesthesia team through an anesthesia machine and scavenging system. Monitor airway, ventilation, blood pressure, and temperature, and watch for signs of malignant hyperthermia such as rising end-tidal CO2 and rigidity.

name: Sodium Polystyrene Sulfonate
shortExplanation: A resin given by mouth or rectally that removes potassium through the stool to treat high potassium.

sections.mechanism: A cation-exchange resin that binds potassium in the gut in exchange for sodium, which is then eliminated in the stool.
sections.sideEffects: Constipation, nausea, anorexia.
sections.adverseEffects: Rare intestinal necrosis, particularly after surgery or with bowel disease; adds a sodium load.
sections.nursingImplications: Works slowly and is not for emergency lowering of potassium. Assess bowel function and ensure the patient can have a bowel movement. Monitor potassium and sodium. Newer binders such as patiromer are also used.

name: Succinylcholine
shortExplanation: A very fast, short-acting depolarizing paralytic used to relax muscles for intubation. It provides no sedation or analgesia.

sections.mechanism: Depolarizing neuromuscular blocker that continuously stimulates then desensitizes the acetylcholine receptor, causing brief muscle fasciculations followed by paralysis. Very rapid onset and offset.
sections.sideEffects: Muscle fasciculations, post-procedure muscle aches, and a small transient rise in potassium.
sections.adverseEffects: Dangerous hyperkalemia in at-risk patients (burns, crush injury, prolonged immobility, certain neuromuscular disease), malignant hyperthermia in susceptible patients, and bradycardia.
sections.nursingImplications: Confirm no contraindications for hyperkalemia risk before use. Ensure sedation is given because it provides none. Have emergency airway equipment ready; know malignant hyperthermia protocol and dantrolene location.

name: Sugammadex
shortExplanation: A reversal agent that rapidly ends paralysis from rocuronium or vecuronium, commonly used at the end of anesthesia to restore breathing and muscle strength.

sections.mechanism: Encapsulates rocuronium or vecuronium molecules and removes them from the neuromuscular junction, quickly reversing paralysis.
sections.sideEffects: Nausea, vomiting, hypotension, and headache.
sections.adverseEffects: Anaphylaxis and hypersensitivity, bradycardia (sometimes severe), and reduced effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives for a period after the dose.
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor recovery of muscle strength with a train-of-four nerve stimulator and watch for return of adequate breathing. Watch for bradycardia and allergic reactions. Counsel patients on hormonal contraceptives about temporarily reduced efficacy.

name: Surfactant (Exogenous)
shortExplanation: A medication instilled into a premature baby's lungs to replace the natural substance that keeps the air sacs from collapsing.

sections.mechanism: Lowers surface tension inside the alveoli so they stay open at the end of each breath, improving oxygenation and lung compliance.
sections.sideEffects: Transient drop in oxygen saturation, heart rate changes, or reflux of the dose during administration.
sections.adverseEffects: Airway obstruction from the instilled dose, and rarely pulmonary hemorrhage.
sections.nursingImplications: Delivered through the endotracheal tube. Monitor oxygen saturation and heart rate closely during administration and be prepared for transient desaturation. Lung compliance can improve quickly, so ventilator settings and oxygen often need prompt adjustment to avoid overinflation.

name: Vancomycin
shortExplanation: A broad-spectrum antibiotic used to treat serious infections, including resistant bacteria — often started empirically while cultures are pending in suspected sepsis.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis; effective against many gram-positive organisms including MRSA. Requires trough-level monitoring for dosing and renal function tracking.
sections.sideEffects: Redness/flushing with rapid infusion ("red man syndrome"), phlebitis at the infusion site.
sections.adverseEffects: Nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, severe infusion reactions if given too quickly.
sections.nursingImplications: Infuse slowly over at least 60 minutes, monitor trough levels and renal function, watch for signs of red man syndrome.

name: Vasopressin
shortExplanation: A hormone given as a fixed-dose infusion to raise blood pressure in shock, usually added to norepinephrine in septic shock.

sections.mechanism: Acts on vascular V1 receptors to constrict blood vessels through a pathway separate from catecholamines, raising blood pressure without directly stimulating the heart.
sections.sideEffects: Pallor, abdominal cramping, and hyponatremia.
sections.adverseEffects: Excessive vasoconstriction causing digital, mesenteric, or cardiac ischemia.
sections.nursingImplications: Typically run at a fixed dose (not titrated like other pressors) as an adjunct to norepinephrine. Monitor blood pressure, urine output, and perfusion to the fingers, toes, and gut. Give through a central line when possible.

name: Vinca Alkaloids (class)
shortExplanation: A class of plant-derived chemotherapy drugs, including vincristine and vinblastine, used for leukemias, lymphomas, and other cancers. Peripheral neuropathy is their signature side effect.

sections.mechanism: Bind tubulin and block microtubule assembly, arresting the mitotic spindle so dividing cells cannot complete cell division.
sections.sideEffects: Peripheral neuropathy (numbness, tingling, weakness), constipation and ileus, and hair loss; vinblastine causes more myelosuppression than vincristine.
sections.adverseEffects: Severe or disabling neuropathy, and vesicant tissue injury on extravasation. These drugs are fatal if given intrathecally and must only be given intravenously.
sections.nursingImplications: Give IV only, never into the spinal fluid, and verify labeling carefully. Assess for neuropathy and bowel function, encourage a bowel regimen to prevent constipation, and monitor the IV site for extravasation.

name: Warfarin
shortExplanation: An oral anticoagulant used for long-term prevention of blood clots, commonly in atrial fibrillation or after a DVT/PE.

sections.mechanism: Inhibits vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (II, VII, IX, X). Requires regular INR monitoring due to a narrow therapeutic window and many drug/food interactions.
sections.sideEffects: Bruising, minor bleeding.
sections.adverseEffects: Major bleeding (GI, intracranial) especially if INR is supratherapeutic; skin necrosis (rare, early therapy).
sections.nursingImplications: Monitor INR regularly, educate on consistent vitamin K intake, watch for interacting medications.

name: Arterial Line Insertion
shortExplanation: Placement of a catheter into an artery (commonly radial) for continuous blood pressure monitoring and frequent blood draws without repeated needle sticks.

sections.targetConcern: Need for beat-to-beat blood pressure monitoring, e.g. while titrating a vasopressor, or frequent arterial blood gas sampling.
sections.whatToMonitor: Waveform quality, distal perfusion/pulses of the cannulated limb, insertion site for bleeding, accidental disconnection (risk of significant blood loss).

name: AV Fistula and Graft Care
shortExplanation: Care and protection of the surgically created blood vessel access used to perform hemodialysis.

sections.targetConcern: Provides durable access for hemodialysis needles - a fistula directly joins an artery and vein, while a graft uses a synthetic tube between them.
sections.whatToMonitor: Check for a thrill (a palpable buzz) and listen for a bruit (a whooshing sound) each shift, and assess circulation to the hand. Protect the access limb: no blood pressure cuffs, blood draws, or IVs in that arm. Watch for bleeding, infection, and steal syndrome (a cold, painful hand).

name: Bronchoscopy
shortExplanation: Passing a thin camera-tipped scope into the airways to look inside the lungs, clear secretions or blockages, and collect samples.

sections.targetConcern: Diagnosing and managing airway and lung problems - clearing mucus plugs or blood, sampling for infection or masses (biopsy, bronchoalveolar lavage), and evaluating persistent respiratory issues.
sections.whatToMonitor: Oxygen saturation, heart rate, blood pressure, and respiratory status during and after the procedure. Watch for bleeding, low oxygen, bronchospasm, and pneumothorax. Keep the patient NPO until the gag reflex returns after topical airway anesthesia.

name: Cardiac Ablation
shortExplanation: A catheter is guided to the heart to burn (radiofrequency) or freeze (cryo) the small area of tissue causing an abnormal rhythm — destroying the faulty electrical pathway so a normal rhythm can hold.

sections.targetConcern: Recurrent or drug-refractory arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation, SVT, or ventricular tachycardia originating from an identifiable focus.
sections.whatToMonitor: Access site (usually femoral) for bleeding or hematoma, cardiac rhythm for recurrence or new arrhythmia, signs of cardiac tamponade (hypotension, muffled heart sounds, JVD), distal pulses.

name: Cardiac Stress Test
shortExplanation: Monitors the heart while it's made to work harder — by exercise or medication — to reveal blocked coronary arteries that don't cause symptoms at rest.

sections.targetConcern: Suspected coronary artery disease — evaluating exertional chest pain or risk before certain procedures.
sections.whatToMonitor: ECG for ischemic changes, blood pressure and heart rate response, chest pain or shortness of breath — stop the test for significant symptoms or ECG changes.

name: Central Line Insertion
shortExplanation: Placement of a catheter into a large central vein for reliable IV access — used for vasopressors, certain medications, or when peripheral access is inadequate.

sections.targetConcern: Need for reliable central venous access, e.g. to safely administer vasopressors in septic shock.
sections.whatToMonitor: Insertion site for bleeding/infection, chest x-ray to confirm placement and rule out pneumothorax, signs of catheter-related bloodstream infection.

name: Chemotherapy
shortExplanation: The use of cytotoxic drugs to kill or slow the growth of cancer cells, usually given in cycles. Because it also affects fast-dividing healthy cells, it causes predictable side effects like low blood counts, hair loss, and nausea.

sections.targetConcern: Destroys or controls cancer by targeting rapidly dividing cells; it may be curative, used to shrink tumors before surgery, given after surgery to reduce recurrence, or used for palliation.
sections.whatToMonitor: Complete blood counts for myelosuppression (neutropenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia), signs of infection, nausea and vomiting, mucositis, kidney and liver function, and infusion or hypersensitivity reactions. Watch the IV site closely for vesicant extravasation and monitor for tumor lysis syndrome with bulky, rapidly dividing tumors.

name: Chest Tube Placement
shortExplanation: Insertion of a tube into the pleural space to drain air, blood, or fluid and re-expand the lung — commonly used for pneumothorax or significant pleural effusion.

sections.targetConcern: Pneumothorax or large pleural effusion causing respiratory compromise.
sections.whatToMonitor: Drainage amount/color, air leak (bubbling in the water seal chamber), respiratory status, insertion site for bleeding/infection, subcutaneous emphysema.

name: Continuous Renal Replacement Therapy
shortExplanation: A slow, continuous form of dialysis used in critically ill patients who cannot tolerate the rapid fluid shifts of standard hemodialysis.

sections.targetConcern: Removing fluid, waste, and correcting electrolyte and acid-base imbalances gradually in hemodynamically unstable patients with acute kidney injury, severe fluid overload, or dangerous electrolyte disturbances.
sections.whatToMonitor: Hourly fluid balance and hemodynamics, the dialysis circuit for clotting and pressure alarms, anticoagulation status, and electrolytes (especially potassium, calcium, and phosphorus). Monitor for hypothermia, hypotension, and access-site integrity.

name: Coronary Artery Bypass Graft
shortExplanation: Open-heart surgery that reroutes blood around blocked coronary arteries using a healthy vessel taken from elsewhere in the body — restoring blood supply to heart muscle beyond the blockage.

sections.targetConcern: Severe multi-vessel or left main coronary disease that isn't well suited to stenting, often with angina or reduced heart function.
sections.whatToMonitor: Hemodynamics and cardiac rhythm (arrhythmias are common postoperatively), chest tube output, sternal incision and graft harvest sites for bleeding/infection, respiratory status and pain control, neuro status after bypass.

name: Defibrillation
shortExplanation: An unsynchronized electrical shock delivered to a pulseless, chaotic rhythm (VF or pulseless VT) to stop it and give the heart a chance to restart a normal rhythm.

sections.targetConcern: Ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia — a shockable cardiac arrest rhythm requiring immediate defibrillation.
sections.whatToMonitor: Rhythm and pulse immediately after each shock, quality of CPR between shocks, airway and oxygenation, skin at pad sites.

name: Echocardiogram
shortExplanation: An ultrasound of the heart that shows how well it pumps, how the valves move, and whether there's fluid around it — a painless bedside or lab test.

sections.targetConcern: Need to assess heart function (ejection fraction), valve disease, wall motion after MI, or a pericardial effusion.
sections.whatToMonitor: For a transthoracic study, no special monitoring; for a transesophageal (TEE) study, airway, sedation level, and gag reflex/NPO status before eating.

name: Endotracheal Intubation
shortExplanation: Placement of a breathing tube into the trachea to secure the airway and allow mechanical ventilation — used in respiratory failure or when a patient can't protect their own airway.

sections.targetConcern: Respiratory failure or inability to protect the airway.
sections.whatToMonitor: Tube placement (breath sounds, capnography, chest x-ray), oxygen saturation, blood pressure during and after the procedure, signs of accidental extubation.

name: Epidural Analgesia
shortExplanation: A regional anesthesia technique in which medication is delivered through a small catheter near the spinal nerves to relieve labor pain.

sections.targetConcern: Provides effective pain relief during labor and delivery while keeping the mother awake, and can be dosed further if a cesarean becomes necessary.
sections.whatToMonitor: Watch for maternal hypotension, which is the most common complication and can reduce placental blood flow, so monitor blood pressure frequently and continue fetal heart rate monitoring. Also assess for urinary retention, degree of motor block and fall risk, itching, fever, and postdural puncture headache. A fluid bolus is often given beforehand to reduce hypotension.

name: Fetal Heart Rate Monitoring
shortExplanation: Tracking the baby's heart rate and the mother's contractions during labor to assess how well the fetus is tolerating labor.

sections.targetConcern: Detects signs of fetal hypoxia or distress so the team can intervene before harm occurs, most often using external Doppler and a contraction sensor.
sections.whatToMonitor: Assess baseline rate (normal roughly 110-160 beats per minute), variability, accelerations, and decelerations in relation to contractions. Late decelerations suggest uteroplacental insufficiency, and variable decelerations suggest cord compression. For nonreassuring patterns, reposition the mother, give IV fluids and oxygen, stop oxytocin, and notify the provider.

name: Foley Catheter Insertion
shortExplanation: Placement of an indwelling urinary catheter to drain the bladder and allow accurate output monitoring.

sections.targetConcern: Urinary retention, need for precise hourly output monitoring (e.g. in shock or with diuretic therapy), or immobility complicating toileting.
sections.whatToMonitor: Urine color/clarity/amount, signs of catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI), skin integrity around the insertion site, bladder distension if the catheter appears blocked.

name: General Anesthesia
shortExplanation: A medically induced, reversible state of unconsciousness with loss of sensation and reflexes so surgery can be performed. The airway is usually controlled with an endotracheal tube or supraglottic airway.

sections.targetConcern: Allows major or painful surgery by producing unconsciousness, amnesia, analgesia, and muscle relaxation while the anesthesia team supports breathing and hemodynamics.
sections.whatToMonitor: Airway patency and ventilation, oxygen saturation and end-tidal CO2, blood pressure and heart rate, temperature, and level of consciousness on emergence. Watch for airway obstruction, laryngospasm, hypotension, hypothermia, and postoperative nausea after extubation.

name: Hemodialysis
shortExplanation: Filters waste, excess fluid, and electrolytes from the blood using an external machine — used when the kidneys can no longer do this on their own.

sections.targetConcern: Acute kidney injury or end-stage renal disease with dangerous fluid overload, electrolyte imbalance, or uremia.
sections.whatToMonitor: Blood pressure during treatment (intradialytic hypotension is common), fluid removal amount versus goal, vascular access site (fistula/graft/catheter) patency and infection signs, post-dialysis electrolytes.

name: ICD Placement
shortExplanation: Implantation of a device that continuously watches the heart rhythm and delivers a shock automatically if a life-threatening arrhythmia occurs.

sections.targetConcern: High risk of sudden cardiac death — e.g. survived cardiac arrest, reduced ejection fraction, or dangerous ventricular arrhythmias.
sections.whatToMonitor: Implant pocket for bleeding/hematoma or infection, arm movement restrictions on the implant side, device function and any delivered shocks, signs of lead dislodgement.

name: Lumbar Puncture
shortExplanation: Needle sampling of cerebrospinal fluid from the lower spine — used to diagnose conditions like meningitis or to relieve elevated pressure around the brain.

sections.targetConcern: Suspected CNS infection (e.g. meningitis) or need to measure/relieve elevated intracranial pressure.
sections.whatToMonitor: Post-procedure headache (positional, from CSF leak), neuro checks, insertion site for bleeding or CSF leakage.

name: Moderate Sedation
shortExplanation: Drug-induced depression of consciousness in which the patient responds purposefully to voice or light touch and keeps their own airway and breathing. It is used for procedures such as endoscopy, cardioversion, and line placement.

sections.targetConcern: Provides comfort, anxiolysis, and analgesia for shorter procedures without the airway support and full unconsciousness of general anesthesia.
sections.whatToMonitor: Level of responsiveness, respiratory rate and depth, oxygen saturation, capnography where available, and blood pressure and heart rate. Watch for oversedation and airway obstruction; have oxygen, suction, and reversal agents (naloxone for opioids, flumazenil for benzodiazepines) immediately available.

name: Nasogastric Tube Insertion
shortExplanation: Placement of a tube through the nose into the stomach for gastric decompression, medication delivery, or short-term enteral feeding.

sections.targetConcern: Bowel obstruction requiring decompression, inability to take oral intake, or need for short-term enteral nutrition/medication access.
sections.whatToMonitor: Placement confirmation (x-ray and/or aspirate pH), drainage amount/color, nasal and throat skin integrity, aspiration risk during feeds.

name: Ostomy Care
shortExplanation: The care of a surgical stoma that diverts stool or urine into an external pouch, including skin protection and output monitoring.

sections.targetConcern: Manages a colostomy, ileostomy, or urostomy - a surgically created opening (stoma) that routes waste into an external appliance.
sections.whatToMonitor: A healthy stoma is pink to red and moist; report a dusky, pale, or black stoma immediately. Protect the surrounding (peristomal) skin, ensure a good pouch seal, and monitor output, since high-volume ileostomy output can cause dehydration and electrolyte loss.

name: Pacemaker Insertion
shortExplanation: Implantation of a small device under the skin with leads into the heart that deliver electrical impulses to keep the heart beating at an adequate rate.

sections.targetConcern: Symptomatic bradycardia, high-grade heart block, or another conduction problem where the heart's own rate is too slow to meet the body's needs.
sections.whatToMonitor: Insertion pocket for bleeding/hematoma or infection, heart rate and rhythm to confirm capture, arm movement restrictions on the implant side, signs of lead dislodgement (hiccups, failure to pace).

name: Packed Red Blood Cell Transfusion
shortExplanation: Infusion of donor red blood cells to treat significant blood loss or anemia that's causing symptoms or instability.

sections.targetConcern: Symptomatic anemia or acute blood loss where the patient's own red cell count is too low to meet oxygen delivery needs.
sections.whatToMonitor: Vital signs closely (especially the first 15 minutes), signs of transfusion reaction (fever, chills, rash, back pain, dyspnea) — stop the transfusion immediately and notify the provider if suspected.

name: Paracentesis
shortExplanation: Needle drainage of fluid from the abdominal cavity — relieves pressure from ascites and can help identify its cause.

sections.targetConcern: Large-volume ascites causing abdominal distension, discomfort, or respiratory compromise; or ascites of unclear cause needing diagnostic sampling.
sections.whatToMonitor: Vital signs for hypotension from fluid shifts (especially with large-volume taps), insertion site for leakage, need for albumin replacement after large-volume removal.

name: PEG Tube Placement
shortExplanation: Endoscopic placement of a feeding tube directly through the abdominal wall into the stomach — used when a patient needs long-term enteral nutrition.

sections.targetConcern: Inability to safely swallow or take adequate oral nutrition long-term (e.g. after stroke, in progressive neurologic disease).
sections.whatToMonitor: Stoma site for infection/leakage, tube placement before each feed, feeding tolerance (nausea, distension), skin integrity around the site.

name: Percutaneous Coronary Intervention
shortExplanation: Threading a catheter through an artery to open a blocked coronary vessel — a balloon widens the narrowing and a stent is usually left behind to hold it open, restoring blood flow to the heart.
